1697	with $a_j$ pieces of width $m^j$.  Apply
1698	Proposition~\ref{prop:power-interchange} to each corresponding pair.
1699	All these calls use the same row field of length $R'$, which is divisible
1700	by each required $W^j$.  At completion every call preserves its row
1701	address, so it neither mixes genuine rows with padded rows nor depends
1702	on the values used for padding.  The padded zero rows remain zero at
1703	these completed-call boundaries.  The sum of the costs is bounded by
1704	\[
1705	 O(V)\sum_j a_jm^{j\tau}=O(Ve^\tau).
1706	\]
1707	The fixed bound $a_j<m$ and the inequality $m^k<me$ make this a
1708	geometric sum of the stated order.  Scan away the padded rows, then
1709	reverse only the moves that joined the high parts.  This is the last
1710	transition in the field-order display: $h^+$ returns to the later
1711	high position, while $d^+$ stays in the earlier one.  The final order
1712	is therefore the required interchange of the two full chunks.  The
1713	remaining movement cost $O(V\log(2e))$ is $O(Ve^\tau)$.
1714	Computing the piece list and every new shape is polynomial in
1715	$\log(2V)$ per piece.  There are at most
1716	$(m-1)(k+1)=O(\log(2e))$ pieces; since $V\ge q^{2e}$, their total
1717	descriptor cost is a fixed power of $\log(2V)$ and hence $O(V)$.
1718	Each power-width call uses the fixed schedule proved above and leaves
1719	its work tapes clean.
1720	
1721	Finally, for binary chunks let $e$ be the least integer with
1722	$q^e\ge2^u$.  Pad each of the two chunk ranges numerically from $[2^u]$
1723	to $[q^e]$, putting zero in an entry if either chunk coordinate is
1724	invalid.  The increase in volume is less than $q^2$, a fixed factor.
1725	The padding is a nested scan through consecutive valid and invalid
1726	intervals, with their lengths prepared from the shape.  It costs $O(V)$
1727	with a constant depending on $q$.  Lexicographic radix-$q$ order of
1728	$[q^e]$ is its numerical order, just as binary order of $[2^u]$ is its
1729	numerical order.  Padding therefore preserves the order of the existing
1730	entries without converting the digits of every address.
1731	The completed interchange preserves the set on which both chunk
1732	coordinates lie below $2^u$.  Scan away the other entries to recover the
1733	desired binary array.  Since $e=O(u)$ for fixed $q$, the bound is
1734	$O(Vu^\tau)$.
1735	\end{proof}

1737	The lemma permits arbitrary prefix, gap, and suffix lengths.  Thus every
1738	later interchange of equal bit chunks is an instance of its stated
1739	layout, after multiplying the irrelevant contiguous lengths.
1740	For widths differing by one bit, choose the leading bit of the longer
1741	chunk as the extra bit.  Suppress the outer prefix and suffix, and write
1742	$g$ for the intervening address field.  If the first chunk is longer,
1743	write it as $(h_0,H)$, so $H$ and the second chunk $D$ have equal width.
1744	The physical orders are
1745	\[
1746	 (h_0,H,g,D)\longmapsto(h_0,D,g,H)
1747	              \longmapsto(D,g,h_0,H).
1748	\]
1749	The first step interchanges $H,D$ by the lemma; the second moves the
1750	single bit $h_0$ immediately before $H$.  If the second chunk is longer,
1751	write it as $(d_0,D)$, with $H$ the first chunk.  Use
1752	\[
1753	 (H,g,d_0,D)\longmapsto(d_0,H,g,D)
1754	              \longmapsto(d_0,D,g,H).
1755	\]
1756	Here the first step moves $d_0$ immediately before $H$, and the second
1757	interchanges $H,D$.  In each case $g$ remains between the two full chunks
1758	in the final order.  If $H,D$ are empty, the indicated equal-width
1759	interchange is the identity.  Each case uses one single-bit move, costing
1760	$O(V)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:elementary-streams}, in addition to the
1761	equal-width interchange.  No unrestricted array transpose is being used
1762	in these operations.
1763	 \section{Fast simultaneous synthetic butterfly layers}
1764	\label{sec:fast-butterfly-layers}
1765	
1766	We now apply the complex network to a common butterfly layer on several
1767	axes. The array has complete address set
1768	\[
1769	 [P]\times[2^K]^D\times[S],\qquad 1\le D\le d,
1770	\]
1771	with $P,S\ge1$, in lexicographic order. Its $D$ consecutive $K$-bit
1772	chunks each select the bit at one common offset $0\le\rho<K$, counted
1773	from the least significant
1774	end. Each address carries a polynomial record with $r$ complex
1775	coefficients, initially in the unit disk on the grid
1776	$2^{-p}\mathbb Z[i]$, with $\Theta(p)$ bits per real or imaginary
1777	component. The intended operation is the tensor product
1778	of $H_0(u,v)=((u+v)/2,(u-v)/2)$ on the $D$ selected bits, acting
1779	coefficientwise and preserving all other address fields.
1780	
1781	The parameters will satisfy
1782	\[
1783	 d=\Theta(p^\epsilon),\qquad K=\lfloor d^c\rfloor,
1784	 \qquad r=2^{\Theta(p/d)},\qquad c>0,\quad 0<\epsilon<1.
1785	\]
1786	The exponents and comparison constants are fixed, and we impose their
1787	further restrictions in Proposition~\ref{prop:simultaneous-layer}.
1788	Two consequences explain the layout. The polynomial length $r$ grows
1789	faster than every fixed power of $p$, so a scan of a record pays for
1790	polynomial work on its address. Also $K/\log p\to\infty$, which will
1791	make the exceptional set in a packed change of address bits small enough
1792	to repair by sorting. We will obtain cost $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$, with
1793	$\lambda'<1$ and $V$ the logical bit volume, whereas separate butterfly
1794	factors would require $D$ whole-array passes.
1795	
1796	We first construct tensor products of the auxiliary two-point kernel
1797	$C$ from Proposition~\ref{prop:complex-motif-interface}. Its phase
1798	frames express a $C$ tensor product using smaller groups of
1799	selected bits, separated by binary changes of basis. We implement those
1800	changes by moving whole address chunks. Splitting complete rows among
1801	the network's wire roles then reduces the volume of each recursive
1802	call. Finally, we bound the intermediate dyadic values and convert the
1803	completed $C$ layer to the normalized $H_0$ layer. The entire layer is
1804	evaluated exactly before one final truncation.
1805	
1806	\subsection{Phase frames for a simultaneous butterfly layer}
1807	\label{subsec:phase-frames}
1808	
1809	Hold the unselected address bits fixed and regard the stored complex
1810	values on one wire role as a function of the selected bits.  The phase
1811	identities below express an edge's residual operator as a product of
1812	two-point kernels on selected directions.
1813	
1814	Put
1815	\[
1816	 H_0=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
1817	 H=\sqrt2 H_0,\qquad \mathsf S=\operatorname{diag}(1,i),\qquad
1818	 Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1).
1819	\]
1820	For the bit-flip matrix $X=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
1821	define
1822	\begin{equation}\label{eq:phase-C}
1823	 C=H\mathsf SH=aI+bX,\qquad a=\frac{1+i}{2},\quad b=\frac{1-i}{2}.
1824	\end{equation}
1825	Direct multiplication gives
1826	\begin{equation}\label{eq:phase-basic-identities}
1827	 H_0=b\mathsf SC\mathsf S,\qquad C^2=X,\qquad C^4=I,\qquad
1828	 C^{-1}=bI+aX=-iZCZ.
1829	\end{equation}
1830	In particular, $C=iZC^{-1}Z$.  These identities use only Gaussian dyadic
1831	coefficients.  The Hadamard matrices in the definition of
1832	$\mathcal C_U$ are used to prove identities; they need not be executed
1833	by the machine.
1834	
1835	Consider an edge from label $U_-$ to label $U_+$, and choose an
1836	orthonormal basis $v_1,\ldots,v_{\rho_{\rm edge}}$ of its residual.
1837	Proposition~\ref{prop:complex-motif-interface} gives the frame change
1838	\[
1839	 \mathcal C_{U_+}\mathcal C_{U_-}^{-1}
1840	 =\prod_{j=1}^{\rho_{\rm edge}}(aI+bX_{v_j})^{\epsilon_j},
1841	 \qquad \epsilon_j\in\{1,-1\}.
1842	\]
1843	Here $(X_vf)(x)=f(x+v)$, and we write $C_v=aI+bX_v$.
1844	The number of directional kernels is precisely
1845	$\rho_{\rm edge}$, including on decreasing edges. The next step puts those directions
1846	into coordinate positions without performing a general transpose.
1847	
1848	\paragraph{Implementing an arbitrary residual basis.}
1849	For $M\in\operatorname{GL}(m,\mathbb F_2)$, let $\mathcal P_M$ be the
1850	address permutation that moves the value at $x$ to $Mx$.  Thus
1851	$(\mathcal P_Mf)(x)=f(M^{-1}x)$, and
1852	\begin{equation}\label{eq:phase-conjugation}
1853	 \mathcal P_MX_v\mathcal P_M^{-1}=X_{Mv}.
1854	\end{equation}
1855	Extend $v_1,\ldots,v_{\rho_{\rm edge}}$ to a basis of $\mathbb F_2^m$ and take these vectors as
1856	the first $\rho_{\rm edge}$ columns of $M$.  The displayed edge identity
1857	then becomes
1858	\begin{equation}\label{eq:phase-edge-coordinate}
1859	 \mathcal C_{U_+}\mathcal C_{U_-}^{-1}
1860	 =\mathcal P_M\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\rho_{\rm edge}}C_{e_j}^{\epsilon_j}\right)
1861	   \mathcal P_M^{-1},
1862	\end{equation}
1863	where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector.  The matrix $M$ need not
1864	preserve the dot product: equation~\eqref{eq:phase-conjugation} only
1865	uses its invertibility.
1866	
1867	For the array layout used below, take a group of $e=mf$ consecutive
1868	axis chunks and divide it into $m$ consecutive slots of $f$ chunks,
1869	numbered in physical order.
1870	Number the chunks within each slot by $j=0,\ldots,f-1$, starting at
1871	its least significant end.  Write $x_{h,j}$ for the selected bit in
1872	chunk $j$ of slot $h$, where $1\le h\le m$.  Column $j$ is the vector
1873	$(x_{1,j},\ldots,x_{m,j})$.  A frame on this group is the tensor
1874	product of the same phase frame
1875	$\mathcal C_U$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:complex-motif-interface}
1876	on these $f$ columns.
1877	
1878	To implement \eqref{eq:phase-edge-coordinate} on the group, first apply
1879	$\mathcal P_M^{-1}$ separately to each column.  For each
1880	$1\le h\le\rho_{\rm edge}$, apply $(C^{\epsilon_h})^{\otimes f}$ to the
1881	$f$ bits $x_{h,0},\ldots,x_{h,f-1}$.  This is one child operation
1882	on the $f$ axes in slot $h$.  Finally apply $\mathcal P_M$ to every
1883	column.  A negative directional kernel still requires only one
1884	forward child, because
1885	\begin{equation}\label{eq:phase-inverse-child}
1886	 (C^{-1})^{\otimes f}
1887	 =(-i)^f Z^{\otimes f}C^{\otimes f}Z^{\otimes f}.
1888	\end{equation}
1889	The rightmost phase is applied first.  All inverse wrappers are address
1890	signs and constant fourth-root phases, so they add no recursive calls.
1891	
1892	Gaussian elimination expresses any $M\in\operatorname{GL}(m,\mathbb F_2)$
1893	as a product of at most $m(m-1)+3m$ elementary row additions: one clears
1894	at most $m-1$ other entries per pivot, and each row swap is three row
1895	additions.  Reversing the elimination gives the required product since
1896	each row addition is an involution.  The number is a constant because
1897	$m$ is fixed.  Adding row $h'$ to row $h$ in every column applies
1898	$x_{h,j}\leftarrow x_{h,j}\mathbin\oplus x_{h',j}$ for every
1899	$0\le j<f$.  Thus one row addition changes corresponding selected
1900	positions in two whole slots.  The packed address operation proved
1901	below performs all of these XORs together.
1902	
1903	\paragraph{The exact recursive contract.}
1904	Apply the finite network with these column frames to a group of
1905	$e=mf$ selected axes.  Summing its residual dimensions gives exactly
1906	$s_{\rm c}$ child calls, each on the $f=e/m$ axes of one slot.
1907	The source and sink $Z_{a,f}$ signs, together with the scalar
1908	$i^{27f}$ at each affected sink, turn every endpoint kernel into a
1909	forward one.  Negating the prescribed physical bank
1910	and undoing its exchange returns each result to its original role.
1911	Proposition~\ref{prop:complex-motif-interface} therefore gives
1912	$C^{\otimes e}$ on every role, including roles whose initial scratch
1913	values were arbitrary.  Formula~\eqref{eq:phase-inverse-child} supplies
1914	each inverse child from one forward call, and none of the corrections
1915	adds a child.  The remaining operations are a fixed number of binary
1916	row additions and coefficientwise scalar operations.
1917	
1918	\paragraph{Returning to normalized butterflies.}
1919	For an address $x$ in a full layer, write $x_1,\ldots,x_D$ for its
1920	selected bits.
1921	The diagonal operator $\mathcal S_D$ multiplies the value stored at
1922	an address by the phase determined by those bits:
1923	\[
1924	 (\mathcal S_D z)(x)=i^{x_1+\cdots+x_D}z(x).
1925	\]
1926	Here the unselected address bits are unchanged, and the same phase is
1927	applied to every coefficient stored at that address.  Applying
1928	\eqref{eq:phase-basic-identities} on all selected coordinates gives
1929	\begin{equation}\label{eq:phase-butterfly-layer}
1930	 H_0^{\otimes D}=b^D\mathcal S_D C^{\otimes D}\mathcal S_D.
1931	\end{equation}
1932	The scalar is
1933	\[
1934	 b^D=(-i/2)^{\lfloor D/2\rfloor}b^{D\bmod2},
1935	\]
1936	so it is a binary shift and fourth-root phase, with at most one further
1937	factor $b$.  All phases, inverse wrappers, and scalar corrections above
1938	are exact Gaussian dyadic operations.  Thus, once the physical binary
1939	basis changes and recursive stream layout are supplied, the complete
1940	parallel butterfly layer is exact up to its prescribed final truncation.
1941	
1942	\subsection{Packed changes of selected address bits}
1943	\label{sec:packed-selected-bits}
1944	
1945	We implement a binary row addition on corresponding selected bits in two
1946	address chunks. A third chunk supplies temporary address bits; its arbitrary
1947	initial value must be restored. The construction first uses a constant number
1948	of cyclic shifts of whole chunk ranges, then corrects an explicitly bounded set of
1949	addresses. The correction depends only on addresses, so the time bound is
1950	worst-case over all payloads.
1951	
1952	We use three previously established streaming operations.
1953	Lemma~\ref{lem:chunk-swap} exchanges two disjoint address chunks of
1954	equal width $L$ in $O(VL^\tau)$ time, where $V$ is the current stream
1955	volume and $0<\tau<1$ is fixed.  The construction in
1956	Lemma~\ref{lem:ordered-affine-streams} cyclically shifts the complete
1957	range of a target chunk by an offset determined by preceding fields in
1958	$O(V)$ time apart from calculating the offsets.  Finally,
1959	Lemma~\ref{lem:elementary-streams} applies any fixed permutation to the
1960	two-bit value at two specified address positions in $O(V)$ time.
1961	Each operation uses a fixed number of one-dimensional
1962	tapes and restores the order of all spectator fields.
1963	
1964	The asymptotic simplification in the following lemma describes a fixed
1965	family of parameters as \(p\to\infty\), after the exponents and comparison
1966	constants have been fixed.  The statement that \(R\) exceeds every fixed
1967	polynomial in \(p\) means that \(R/p^C\to\infty\) for each fixed \(C\).
1968	Implied constants and eventual cutoffs may depend on the fixed choices
1969	and on when the family's asserted bounds begin to hold.  In particular,
1970	each explicit bound is uniform over all of its declared inputs;
1971	its asymptotic simplification is uniform over the allowed row counts
1972	and payloads within a fixed family.
1973	
1974	\begin{lemma}[Packed selected-bit addition on one rectangle]
1975	\label{lem:packed-selected-bit-rectangle}
1976	Let $R\ge1$, $K\ge6$, $f\ge1$, $L=fK$, and $0\le\rho<K$.
1977	Let $N_0,N_1,N_2,N_3$ be positive integers, and let
1978	$(\chi_1,\chi_2,\chi_3)$ be a permutation of $(x,y,z)$.
1979	Consider $R$-bit records in lexicographic order on
1980	\[
1981	 [N_0]\times[2^L]_{\chi_1}\times[N_1]\times[2^L]_{\chi_2}
1982	 \times[N_2]\times[2^L]_{\chi_3}\times[N_3].
1983	\]
1984	The subscript names the chunk at that position. The input supplies
1985	$N_0,\ldots,N_3,R,K,f,\rho$ as a fixed number of canonical binary
1986	integers, together with the finite permutation of the chunk names, as
1987	in Section~\ref{sec:streams}. Put
1988	\[
1989	 M=2^{3L}\prod_{h=0}^3N_h,\qquad V=MR,\qquad
1990	 A_{\rm rect}=\lceil\log_2(2V)\rceil.
1991	\]
1992	At the selected positions $j_i=\rho+iK$, numbered from the least
1993	significant bit, one fixed multitape procedure performs
1994	\[
1995	 y_{j_i}\longleftarrow y_{j_i}\mathbin\oplus x_{j_i}
1996	 \quad(0\le i<f).
1997	\]
1998	It preserves the spectator coordinates, all other chunk bits, and every
1999	record payload; in particular, it restores the entire chunk $z$ for
2000	every initial value.
2001	With $\delta_{\rm bad}=\min\{1,80(f-1)2^{-K}\}$, its time is
2002	\begin{equation}
2003	\label{eq:packed-rectangle-time}
2004	 O\!\left(V(L^\tau+1)+MA_{\rm rect}^3+
2005	       \delta_{\rm bad}MA_{\rm rect}(R+A_{\rm rect})\right).
2006	\end{equation}
2007	When $A_{\rm rect}=O(p)$, $R$ exceeds every fixed polynomial in $p$,
2008	$f\le d\le p$, and $K/\log p\to\infty$, this is
2009	$O(V(L^\tau+1))$, uniformly over the permitted lengths and payloads
2010	in the fixed family.
2011	\end{lemma}
2012	
2013	\begin{proof}
2014	We first construct eight rotations that have the required effect away
2015	from a small set of addresses. We then correct exactly that set.
2016	For a Boolean control $c$ and arbitrary integers $u,w$, perform the following
2017	eight operations in the displayed chronological order. Every predicate
2018	uses the current values of the integers.
2019	\begin{equation}
2020	\label{eq:eight-packed-additions}
2021	\begin{array}{rcl@{\qquad}l}
2022	u&\leftarrow&u-c[\,w\equiv0\pmod2\,],&(1)\\
2023	w&\leftarrow&w-c[\,u\equiv0\pmod2\,],&(2)\\
2024	u&\leftarrow&u+c[\,w\equiv0\pmod2\,],&(3)\\
2025	w&\leftarrow&w+c[\,u\equiv0\pmod2\,],&(4)\\
2026	w&\leftarrow&w+c[\,u\equiv1\pmod2\,],&(5)\\
2027	u&\leftarrow&u+c[\,w\equiv1\pmod2\,],&(6)\\
2028	w&\leftarrow&w-c[\,u\equiv1\pmod2\,],&(7)\\
2029	u&\leftarrow&u-c[\,w\equiv1\pmod2\,].&(8)
2030	\end{array}
2031	\end{equation}
2032	If $c=0$, these operations do nothing. If $c=1$, the first four operations
2033	induce the cycle $(00\ 01\ 10)$ in every square
2034	\[
2035	 \{2a,2a+1\}\times\{2b,2b+1\},\qquad a,b\in\mathbb Z,
2036	\]
2037	where the corner labels record the parities of $(u,w)$. The last four
2038	induce $(01\ 10\ 11)$. Applying the first cycle and then the second gives
2039	$(00\ 10)(01\ 11)$. These facts follow by substituting the four parity
2040	pairs into the displayed operations; translation by $(2a,2b)$ does not
2041	change any predicate. Consequently the complete output is
2042	\begin{equation}
2043	\label{eq:eight-packed-result}
2044	 (u',w')=
2045	 \bigl(u+c(1-2(u\bmod2)),\ w\bigr).
2046	\end{equation}
2047	Here $u\bmod2\in\{0,1\}$, also for negative $u$. Thus the parity of $u$
2048	is flipped precisely when $c=1$, both quotients under division by two are
2049	preserved, and the arbitrary auxiliary integer $w$ is restored. Each
2050	coordinate is updated four times by at most one, so its displacement
2051	from its initial value is at most four, even if an intermediate point
2052	leaves its starting quotient square. The weaker bound eight will suffice below.
2053	
2054	Omit the most significant selected position $j_{f-1}$ temporarily. For
2055	each $0\le i<f-1$, the bits in positions
2056	$j_i,\ldots,j_i+K-1$ form a $K$-bit segment. When $f>1$, these segments
2057	are disjoint, and the highest one ends immediately below $j_{f-1}$.
2058	Write their initial values in $y$ and $z$ as
2059	\[
2060	 u_i=2g_i+a_i,\qquad w_i=2h_i+b_i,
2061	 \qquad a_i,b_i\in\{0,1\}.
2062	\]
2063	The values $g_i,h_i\in\{0,\ldots,2^{K-1}-1\}$ are the guard values. The
2064	control for this pair of segments is the selected bit $c_i=x_{j_i}$.
2065	
2066	Apply each line of \eqref{eq:eight-packed-additions} simultaneously to all
2067	these segment pairs. Physically, a line updating $y$ by sign $\varepsilon$
2068	and testing parity $b$ of $z$ is the single cyclic shift
2069	\begin{equation}
2070	\label{eq:packed-cyclic-shift}
2071	 y\longleftarrow y+
2072	 \varepsilon\sum_{i=0}^{f-2}2^{j_i}
2073	 [\,x_{j_i}=1\,][\,z_{j_i}=b\,]
2074	 \pmod{2^L}.
2075	\end{equation}
2076	For a line updating $z$, interchange $y$ and $z$ in this formula.
2077	The shift offset never depends on its target chunk, so each line is a
2078	bijection of the rectangle. Let $S_0$ be their composition. It fixes
2079	the spectator coordinates.
2080	
2081	Let $\mathcal B$ consist of the addresses for which
2082	at least one used guard value, in either $y$ or $z$, fails
2083	\begin{equation}
2084	\label{eq:packed-guard-interval}
2085	 10\le g\le 2^{K-1}-11.
2086	\end{equation}
2087	At an address outside $\mathcal B$, each segment initially lies in
2088	$[20,2^K-21]$. Even displacement eight keeps it inside
2089	$[0,2^K-1]$. Inductively, each packed addition therefore agrees with all
2090	the independent segment additions: no segment carries into or borrows
2091	from the next segment. When $f>1$, the bits below $j_0$ and above the
2092	highest used segment are untouched as well. By
2093	\eqref{eq:eight-packed-result}, $S_0$
2094	then agrees with the ideal permutation $T_0$ that performs the required

2105	each choice of spectator coordinates. No record value enters this count.
2106	
2107	The ideal map $T_0$ preserves all guard values and therefore preserves
2108	$\mathcal B$. Both $T_0$ and $S_0$ are bijections, and they agree off
2109	$\mathcal B$. Taking complements in the finite rectangle gives
2110	\[
2111	 S_0(\mathcal B^c)=T_0(\mathcal B^c)=\mathcal B^c,
2112	 \qquad S_0(\mathcal B)=\mathcal B.
2113	\]
2114	Thus $T_0S_0^{-1}$ fixes $\mathcal B^c$ and permutes $\mathcal B$.
2115	It remains to implement the rotations and this correction on tapes.
2116	
2117	For one rotation, move its target to the rightmost of the three chunk
2118	positions if necessary. Let $P^{\rm sw}$ be the product of the record
2119	field lengths before the earlier exchanged chunk, let $G^{\rm sw}$
2120	be the product between the exchanged chunks, and let $B^{\rm sw}$ be
2121	$R$ times the product after the later one. Empty products are one.
2122	The bit array has exactly the shape
2123	\[
2124	 [P^{\rm sw}]\times[2^L]\times[G^{\rm sw}]
2125	       \times[2^L]\times[B^{\rm sw}].
2126	\]
2127	The third chunk lies inside one collapsed spectator interval.
2128	Pass only $L$ and these three positive canonical lengths to
2129	Lemma~\ref{lem:chunk-swap}. Each length is at most $V$, so the local
2130	descriptor has $O(A_{\rm rect})$ bits. The swap costs $O(VL^\tau)$, including
2131	its own padding and cleanup.
2132	
2133	The equal chunk lengths leave the field-length list unchanged by a
2134	completed swap. Keep the permutation of the logical names $x,y,z$ in
2135	finite local state. With the target now after its two controls, collapse
2136	the remaining intervals to obtain
2137	\[
2138	 [\Lambda_0]\times[2^L]_{\rm control\,1}\times[\Lambda_1]
2139	 \times[2^L]_{\rm control\,2}\times[\Lambda_2]
2140	 \times[2^L]_{\rm target}\times[B_{\rm rot}],
2141	\]
2142	where $B_{\rm rot}$ includes the payload and every displayed spectator
2143	length is positive. Their product with the chunk lengths is $V$.
2144	Together with $K,f,\rho$ and the finite name permutation, these fixed
2145	canonical lengths form an $O(A_{\rm rect})$-bit local descriptor. The offset
2146	routine receives the two current $L$-bit logical control values. A scan
2147	of at most $f\le L$ selected positions evaluates
2148	\eqref{eq:packed-cyclic-shift} in $L^{O(1)}$ time, without reading the
2149	target or spectator values. Lemma~\ref{lem:ordered-affine-streams}
2150	therefore gives an $O(V)$ rotation: its offset work is absorbed by the
2151	$2^L$ nonempty target blocks in each fiber. Undo the swap after the
2152	rotation. The local descriptors and name permutation are updated at
2153	completed swap boundaries; the primitives use their own descriptors
2154	inside padded layouts.
2155	There are at most sixteen swaps and eight rotations in $S_0$.
2156	
2157	To implement the correction, scan the stream with a record-rank counter.
2158	All chunk names are back in their original positions. Dividing the
2159	current rank through the fixed seven field lengths recovers the three
2160	chunk values and their mixed-radix record strides. The strides exclude
2161	the $R$ payload bits. All involved integers have $O(A_{\rm rect})$ bits, so
2162	schoolbook arithmetic, descriptor copying, and resets take at most
2163	$O(A_{\rm rect}^3)$ per record. Test membership in $\mathcal B$ and extract just
2164	those records. For a current exceptional address $q$, compute
2165	$q'=T_0(S_0^{-1}(q))$ by reversing the eight modular additions with
2166	negated offsets, then applying the selected XORs directly. Each reversed
2167	mask uses the current controls of that reversed line. There are at most
2168	$f\le L\le A_{\rm rect}$ selected positions, so this calculation also fits
2169	$O(A_{\rm rect}^3)$ time.
2170	
2171	If $q_h,q'_h$ are the current and destination values of chunk
2172	$h\in\{x,y,z\}$ and $\sigma_h$ is its record stride, the fixed
2173	spectator coordinates give
2174	\[
2175	 \operatorname{rank}(q')=\operatorname{rank}(q)+
2176	       \sum_{h\in\{x,y,z\}}(q'_h-q_h)\sigma_h.
2177	\]
2178	The differences are signed. Attach this destination rank, padded to
2179	$\lceil\log_2M\rceil\le A_{\rm rect}$ bits, to the extracted record, and mark its
2180	hole on a fixed track of the full stream. Hold the full stream untouched
2181	while stable binary radix sorting scans only the extracted records and
2182	keys, least significant key bit first. Since $T_0S_0^{-1}$ permutes
2183	$\mathcal B$, these keys are distinct and are exactly the ranks of the
2184	marked holes. One forward full-stream scan reinserts the sorted records.
2185	This implements $T_0$ everywhere.
2186	
2187	Finally apply the two-bit XOR to $x_{j_{f-1}},y_{j_{f-1}}$ by
2188	Lemma~\ref{lem:elementary-streams}, splitting those chunks at the
2189	selected positions and collapsing the other intervals. Its descriptor
2190	again has a fixed number of positive lengths, each at most $V$.
2191	This costs $O(V)$ and supplies the omitted selected position. When
2192	$f=1$, $S_0,T_0$ are identities, $\mathcal B$ is empty, and this last
2193	step is the entire algorithm.
2194	
2195	The movement costs $O(V(L^\tau+1))$. A fixed number of full record scans
2196	costs $O(MA_{\rm rect}^3+V)$, and the at most $A_{\rm rect}$ radix passes cost
2197	$O(|\mathcal B|A_{\rm rect}(R+A_{\rm rect}))$; skip them when the extracted bank is empty.
2198	The initial descriptor has a fixed number of canonical integers of
2199	$O(A_{\rm rect})$ bits, so its preparation is covered by $O(MA_{\rm rect}^3)$.
2200	All counters, positioning, rewinds, and cleanup are included.
2201	Equation~\eqref{eq:packed-bad-fraction} proves
2202	\eqref{eq:packed-rectangle-time} on a fixed number of tapes.
2203	After division by $V=MR$, its additional terms are bounded by
2204	$A_{\rm rect}^3/R$ and
2205	$80(f-1)2^{-K}A_{\rm rect}(1+A_{\rm rect}/R)$. Under the stated family bounds
2206	the first tends to zero, and the second is
2207	$O(p^2 2^{-K}(1+A_{\rm rect}/R))=o(1)$. This proves the final assertion.
2208	\end{proof}

2210	\paragraph{Application to a fixed binary change of basis.}
2211	An invertible matrix over $\mathbb F_2$ of fixed order $m\ge3$ is a
2212	product of a fixed number of elementary row additions; a row exchange
2213	is three such additions.  In one invocation of the finite network on
2214	$e=mf$ axes, slot $h$ consists of $f$ consecutive $K$-bit axis chunks.
2215	It therefore has address-bit width $L=fK$, and its selected bits
2216	$x_{h,j}$ occupy positions $\rho+jK$ for $0\le j<f$.
2217	To add row $h'$ to row $h$, use slot $h'$ as $x$,
2218	slot $h$ as $y$, and any third, distinct slot as $z$ in
2219	Lemma~\ref{lem:packed-selected-bit-rectangle}.  The lemma performs
2220	$x_{h,j}\leftarrow x_{h,j}\mathbin\oplus x_{h',j}$ for every $j$ in
2221	one operation and restores the third slot, whatever its initial
2222	address value.
2223	
2224	Under the asymptotic hypotheses in the final assertion of that lemma,
2225	the complete change of basis and its inverse therefore cost
2226	$O(V((eK)^\tau+1))$ on a stream of volume $V$.  Here $e$ counts
2227	axis chunks, while $eK$ counts address bits; the fixed factor $m$
2228	between $eK$ and the slot width does not affect the bound.  The same
2229	conclusion holds after the row padding and splitting below, because
2230	every role stream retains a complete suffix with the same fixed field
2231	lengths in every row.
2232	
2233	\subsection{Batching a common layer on a fixed number of tapes}
2234	
2235	We now turn the finite complex network into an algorithm for a whole
2236	layer.  Throughout this subsection its constants are denoted by
2237	\(m,W,s\): the network has \(W\) wires, its binary label space has
2238	dimension \(m\), and the sum of the dimensions of its edge residuals is
2239	\(s<Wm\).  These are the constants of the complex network; they need not
2240	equal the constants used to prove the chunk-swap lemma.
2241	
2242	Use the complete layout and parameter family specified at the start of
2243	the section, with fixed rational exponents \(c,\epsilon\) to satisfy
2244	the recurrence and guard conditions below. Store each polynomial in
2245	coefficient order with a common width \(w=\Theta(p)\) per real or
2246	imaginary component, and assume the complete address and its binary
2247	shape descriptor have length \(O(p)\). Thus an input record has
2248	\(2rw\) bits. Write \(V\) for the current logical bit volume, excluding
2249	temporary work streams. We first count the work on \(C^{\otimes D}\)
2250	assuming one common exact coefficient format of width \(O(p)\); the
2251	guard calculation below then supplies that format.
2252	
2253	\paragraph{An individual selected-bit kernel.}
2254	Write each input coefficient once in this common exact format and retain it until
2255	the final truncation.  The input width is \(\Theta(p)\), so the
2256	initial copy costs \(O(V)\) and the guarded stream has volume \(O(V)\).
2257	
2258	To apply one \(C\) kernel, use the split from
2259	Lemma~\ref{lem:elementary-streams} at the selected address bit.
2260	Call the two streams \(0\) and \(1\) according to that bit.
2261	Because that bit has its complete two-element range, the two streams
2262	have the same remaining address set in the same order.  Their aligned
2263	record addresses therefore differ only in the selected bit, and their
2264	coefficients are still ordered by the same polynomial index.  Scan
2265	each pair of records in that order.  For corresponding complex
2266	coefficients \(u\) from stream \(0\) and \(v\) from stream \(1\), compute
2267	\begin{equation}\label{eq:individual-C-pair}
2268	 C(u,v)=
2269	 \left(\frac{u+v+i(u-v)}2,\,
2270	       \frac{u+v-i(u-v)}2\right).
2271	\end{equation}
2272	Addition, subtraction and halving use the fixed-point conventions of
2273	Section~\ref{sec:streams}; multiplication by \(i\) swaps the real
2274	and imaginary components and changes one sign.  The common guarded
2275	width makes these operations exact.  The coefficient scan costs
2276	\(O(rp)\) per pair of records, linear in their guarded bit length
2277	and including any reversal of bits inside a coefficient.  Write the
2278	first result to stream \(0\) and the second to stream \(1\), both in
2279	coefficient order, then merge
2280	according to the selected bit.  The merge restores the original
2281	lexicographic address order.  The elementary split and merge include
2282	their counters and cleanup and cost \(O(V)\); the paired arithmetic
2283	scan also costs \(O(V)\).  Thus \(e\) individual kernels cost
2284	\(O(Ve)\) on any stream with these complete ranges and record format.
2285	
2286	First consider an internal node containing \(e=m^k\) consecutive
2287	active chunks, with \(k\ge1\).  Split it into \(m\) consecutive slots,
2288	each containing \(e/m\) chunks.
2289	The phase construction supplies one recursive call on a slot for each
2290	vector in an edge residual basis, hence exactly \(s\) calls in one
2291	invocation of the network.  If the logical volume entering this node
2292	is \(V\), binary changes of basis, their inverses, scalar gates,
2293	endpoint corrections and reassembly of the physical banks cost
2294	\[
2295	 O\bigl(V((eK)^\tau+1)\bigr)
2296	\]
2297	at this node.  Each slot has \((e/m)K\) address bits, so
2298	Lemma~\ref{lem:packed-selected-bit-rectangle} gives the stated bound for a row addition.  The
2299	network and all of its \(m\)-dimensional residual bases are fixed,
2300	so the total number of row additions is fixed as well.  At the same
2301	guarded width, the scalar gates cost a constant
2302	number of scans of the current volume.  Address and descriptor
2303	work bounded by any fixed polynomial in \(p\) per record is also
2304	absorbed: its ratio to the record's \(\Theta(rp)\) bits tends to zero.
2305	
2306	\paragraph{Where the rows come from.}
2307	Put
2308	\[
2309	 q_0=\lceil\log_2 W\rceil\,
2310	       \lceil\log_m(2d)\rceil,
2311	 \qquad k_0=\lceil\log_m d\rceil.
2312	\]
2313	If \(D\le q_0\), use individual \(C\) kernels, at cost \(O(V\log d)\).
2314	Otherwise apply \(C\) individually on the selected bits of the first
2315	\(q_0\) chunks, in \(O(V\log d)\) time.  These chunks remain a
2316	complete consecutive address block before all the remaining chunks;
2317	regard their concatenated bits as one row index.  Its range has
2318	length \(R_{\rm row}=2^{q_0K}\ge W^{k_0}\), since \(K\ge1\) for sufficiently
2319	large \(p\) and \(q_0K\ge k_0\log_2W\).  Within each preceding prefix, add
2320	the same number of zero rows to reach the next multiple of \(W^{k_0}\);
2321	the volume grows
2322	by a factor at most two.  At any recursive depth \(j\le k_0\), the
2323	row count is divisible by \(W^{k_0-j}\).
2324	
2325	At a node, write a row index as \(u=Wg+w\), with \(0\le w<W\),
2326	and send that entire row to physical wire role \(w\), indexed there
2327	by \(g\).  Every role stream has the same remaining address shape.
2328	Thus a pointwise gate reads the records with the same \(g\) and the
2329	same remaining address in its touched roles.  The scalar network
2330	allows these role values to be arbitrary, so the split supplies its
2331	scratch roles from existing rows.  Each recursive edge call acts on
2332	one role stream with volume exactly \(1/W\) of its parent's logical
2333	volume.
2334	
2335	Splitting the row index removes no address within a row. Every row in
2336	every role stream, including a padded row, retains the complete suffix
2337	\([2^K]^{D-q_0}\times[S]\) in the same field order and with the same
2338	lengths; inactive chunks remain complete spectator fields. The row
2339	counts also remain equal across preceding prefixes, decreasing by
2340	the same factor \(W\) at each split. The network is invoked only on
2341	these equal rows: their common suffix gives the aligned role addresses
2342	and exact \(V/W\) child volumes above. For each packed call, collapse
2343	the preceding prefix and row index into one field, and collapse the
2344	spectator intervals around its three slots. This gives the rectangle of
2345	Lemma~\ref{lem:packed-selected-bit-rectangle}, whose guard count and
2346	deterministic repair apply to every child.
2347	
2348	The \(W\) role streams use a fixed number of tapes.  Before entering a
2349	child, push the other role streams onto a LIFO work tape, copy the
2350	active stream to a reserved child input area, and clear or reuse the
2351	role areas.  On return, copy the result back and pop the parked
2352	streams, reversing each popped stream when necessary to restore its
2353	order.  The stack head is at its top at every call boundary.  Pushing,
2354	popping, copying, resetting and clearing at this node cost its own
2355	volume times a fixed constant; no step traverses an ancestor's parked
2356	data.  The call descriptor and program counter use a separate stack.
2357	The number of child calls is the fixed integer \(s\), so these costs
2358	are included in the node overhead above.  The fixed-tape chunk-swap
2359	subroutine has its own fixed work areas, reused on every call.
2360	
2361	For each packed call, padding has increased the row count by at most
2362	a factor two and row splitting can only decrease it.  Its active
2363	address still has \(O(p)\) bits. The four collapsed spectator lengths
2364	therefore have \(O(p)\)-bit descriptions. Its record-width parameter
2365	describes a polynomial of \(\Theta(rp)\) bits and has
2366	\(O(\log(rp))=O(p)\) bits as well. These lengths, together with
2367	\(K,f,\rho\) and the finite chunk-name permutation, are precisely the
2368	local descriptor required by
2369	Lemma~\ref{lem:packed-selected-bit-rectangle}. Both the record count
2370	and record width have \(O(p)\)-bit lengths, so its bound uses
2371	\(A_{\rm rect}=\lceil\log_2(2V)\rceil=O(p)\). A selected-position
2372	mask has at most \(DK=O(p)\) bits.
2373	
2374	The binary descriptions of all growing shape parameters have
2375	polynomial length in \(p\).  Each nonempty child stream still contains
2376	a complete length-\(r\) polynomial record.  Its volume therefore
2377	absorbs polynomial descriptor setup at that node, as well as
2378	polynomial address work per record.  Even if every node is counted
2379	separately, there are only \(d^{O(1)}\) nodes: the branching factor
2380	\(s\) is fixed and the depth is at most
2381	\(\lceil\log_m d\rceil\).  Any additional fixed power of \(p\)
2382	from this count is still dominated by \(r\).
2383	
2384	Every completed network invocation applies \(C^{\otimes e}\)
2385	separately to each input row.  Its selected bits lie in the
2386	remaining chunks, disjoint from the bits used by the earlier
2387	preprocessing.  On the genuine rows, those two completed operations
2388	therefore commute.
2389	Each padded zero row is again zero when an invocation finishes, so the
2390	added rows can be deleted after the invocations on the remaining chunks
2391	have completed. Intermediate scratch values may be arbitrary.
2392	
2393	\paragraph{Unrolling the recurrence.}
2394	Fix \(\beta=1/2\), and choose real exponents satisfying
2395	\[
2396	 0<\tau<1,\qquad
2397	 \max\{0,\log_m(s/W)\}\le\sigma<1,
2398	 \qquad \max\{\tau,\sigma\}<\lambda<1,
2399	 \qquad \tau(1+c/\beta)<\lambda.
2400	\]
2401	The exponents can all be chosen rational, with a strict upper bound
2402	in the condition on \(\sigma\).  Stop recursion when
2403	\(e<d^\beta\) and apply the \(e\) \(C\) kernels individually.  If
2404	\(F(e)\) denotes time divided by the current logical stream volume,
2405	then
2406	\[
2407	 F(e)\le (s/W)F(e/m)+O((eK)^\tau+1),
2408	 \qquad F(e)=O(e)\quad(e<d^\beta).
2409	\]
2410	Indeed, the \(s\) child calls are executed on streams of volume
2411	\(V/W\), so their total cost is \(s(V/W)F(e/m)\).  Dividing by
2412	the current volume \(V\) gives the factor \(s/W\).
2413	At an internal node \(e\ge d^\beta\), hence
2414	\(K\le d^c\le e^{c/\beta}\).  The overhead is therefore
2415	\(O(e^{\tau(1+c/\beta)}+1)=O(e^\lambda)\).
2416	Put \(a=s/W\).  Since \(a\le m^\sigma<m^\lambda\), the internal
2417	costs sum to at most
2418	\[
2419	 C e^\lambda\sum_{j\ge0}(a/m^\lambda)^j=O(e^\lambda).
2420	\]
2421	If the leaves after \(j\) levels contain \(u=e/m^j<d^\beta\)
2422	active chunks each, their combined normalized
2423	contribution is at most
2424	\[
2425	 O(a^ju)\le O(e^\sigma u^{1-\sigma})
2426	          \le O(e^\sigma d^{\beta(1-\sigma)}).
2427	\]
2428	The first inequality uses
2429	\(a^j\le m^{j\sigma}=(e/u)^\sigma\).  It also covers \(a<1\)
2430	by taking \(\sigma\ge0\).
2431	
2432	Write \(D-q_0=\sum_j a_jm^j\) in base \(m\), with \(0\le a_j<m\).
2433	Partition the remaining chunks into \(a_j\) consecutive pieces
2434	containing \(m^j\) chunks for each \(j\).
2435	There are at most \((m-1)(1+\lfloor\log_m d\rfloor)\) pieces.
2436	Adding their costs and the row preprocessing gives
2437	\[
2438	 O\!\left(\log(2d)
2439	    \bigl[d^\lambda+d^{\sigma+\beta(1-\sigma)}+1\bigr]\right)
2440	   =O(d^{\lambda'})
2441	\]
2442	for any fixed
2443	\[
2444	 \max\{\lambda,\sigma+\beta(1-\sigma)\}<\lambda'<1.
2445	\]
2446	The case \(D\le q_0\), in which preprocessing would consume all
2447	active chunks, was handled by individual kernels.  Thus all constants
2448	and all tape counts are independent of \(p,d,r\) and the input data.
2449	
2450	\subsection{An explicit guard-width bound}
2451	
2452	The accelerated network is evaluated exactly until an entire
2453	normalized butterfly layer is complete.  Its intermediate operators
2454	need not be contractions.  We now give explicit constants that bound
2455	denominator and magnitude growth within one layer.
2456	
2457	For the complex network, let
2458	\[
2459	 E=64(W+m+1)^3,\qquad B=s+E,
2460	 \qquad \nu=\min\{j\ge1:m^j\ge B\},
2461	\]
2462	and set
2463	\[
2464	 C_1=\max\{20,\nu+3\},\qquad C_0=128mB^2,
2465	 \qquad \Delta=\lceil C_0d^{C_1}\rceil.
2466	\]
2467	For the stated \(h=100\) construction, the complex network has
2468	\[
2469	\begin{split}
2470	 m&=1{,}000{,}000,\\
2471	 W&=1{,}873{,}807{,}244{,}643{,}542{,}670{,}000,\\
2472	 s&=1{,}873{,}807{,}244{,}636{,}671{,}267{,}308{,}000{,}000.
2473	\end{split}
2474	\]
2475	These values give \(m^{10}<B<m^{11}\), hence \(\nu=11\) and
2476	\(C_1=20\).  In fact the bound below needs only exponent fourteen;
2477	the choice twenty leaves an explicit additional margin.
2478	
2479	We measure arithmetic dependency depth using complex additions,
2480	subtractions, halvings, sign changes and multiplication by \(i\).
2481	For a group of \(e\) axes, let \(A(e)\) bound the number of these
2482	operations on any chain from an input coefficient to an intermediate
2483	coefficient in its recursive \(C\)-layer.  A chain follows an operand
2484	into a later arithmetic result.  Work on other coefficients or records
2485	that do not feed this value lies on other chains, even though the
2486	fixed-tape machine executes that work sequentially.  To obtain a
2487	conservative bound, we concatenate all scalar gates and all recursive
2488	edge calls within one network invocation.
2489	
2490	The scalar schedule \eqref{eq:motif-schedule} touches a data wire
2491	at most four times in each of the three stages.  A scratch wire belongs
2492	to one invocation and is touched at most four times there.  Thus every
2493	physical wire occurs in at most twelve scalar gates, and there are
2494	at most \(12W\) gates.  A gate has at most \(W\) inputs and outputs
2495	and coefficients in \(\{0,\pm1,\pm1/2\}\).  One output is a sum of
2496	at most \(W\) terms, each requiring at most one halving and one
2497	addition or subtraction.  Evaluating all outputs from saved inputs
2498	therefore takes at most \(2W^2\) elementary operations.
2499	
2500	For an inverse child, each \(Z^{\otimes f}\) is one sign chosen by
2501	the parity of the selected address bits, and the scalar fourth-root
2502	phase takes at most one sign change and one multiplication by \(i\).
2503	This gives at most \(4s\) operations for the child corrections.
2504	The source, sink and bank corrections take at most \(4W+4\) more.
2505	Calculating the address parities and phase exponents is address or descriptor
2506	work, not arithmetic on coefficients.  Since \(s<Wm\), the total
2507	\(24W^3+4s+4W+4\) is less than
2508	\(E=64(W+m+1)^3\).  Binary address permutations add no coefficient
2509	arithmetic at their interfaces.
2510	
2511	The paired evaluation in \eqref{eq:individual-C-pair} uses at most
2512	eight elementary operations: form the sum and difference, multiply
2513	the difference by \(i\), then form the two half-sums.  We may therefore use
2514	\[
2515	 A(e)\le sA(e/m)+E
2516	 \quad\hbox{at an internal node},\qquad A(e)\le8e
2517	 \quad\hbox{at a leaf}.
2518	\]
2519	The depth estimate concatenates the \(s\) calls, so it uses \(s\).
2520	The factor \(1/W\) in the earlier time recurrence accounted for
2521	their smaller stream volumes.
2522	
2523	There are at most \(k\le\lceil\log_m d\rceil\) internal levels.
2524	For any bound \(x\ge1\), \(sx+E\le(s+E)x=Bx\).
2525	Starting with \(8e\le8d\le8dB\) at a leaf and applying this
2526	inequality through the levels gives the first bound below.
2527	For the second, use \(B\le m^\nu\) and
2528	\[
2529	 B^{k+1}\le B^{\log_m d+2}
2530	          =B^2d^{\log_m B}\le B^2d^\nu.
2531	\]
2532	Thus
2533	\[

2759	 \section{Synthetic transforms and their tape layout}
2760	\label{sec:synthetic-layouts}
2761	
2762	We now implement the normalized Fourier transforms needed for
2763	convolution.  Their entries will be short polynomials in a quotient
2764	where the required roots of unity act by exact signed permutations
2765	of coefficient lists.  We also specify where each frequency entry
2766	is stored, because the opposite transform consumes that same order
2767	after a pointwise product.
2768	
2769	The polynomial roots and radix-two butterflies belong to the fast
2770	polynomial-transform method of Nussbaumer and
2771	Quandalle~\cite{NussbaumerQuandalle1978,Nussbaumer1980}; we use the
2772	form developed in~\cite[Section~2.4 and Lemma~3.2]{HarveyHoeven2021}.
2773	The work here is to apply the simultaneous layers on a suitable tape
2774	layout and retain the resulting frequency order through convolution.
2775	
2776	For an integer $r\geq 2$ that is a power of two, put
2777	\[
2778	 \mathcal R_r=\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1),\qquad
2779	 \left\|\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}z_k y^k\right\|_\infty
2780	       =\max_{0\leq k<r}|z_k|.
2781	\]
2782	We always use representatives of degree less than $r$.  Multiplication
2783	by $y^a$, for any integer $a$, permutes the coefficients and changes
2784	some signs; consequently it is an isometry for this norm.  For arrays
2785	over $\mathcal R_r$, the same notation denotes the maximum over all
2786	coefficients in all entries.  A disk array has norm at most one.  A
2787	$p$-bit grid array has real and imaginary coefficient parts in
2788	$2^{-p}\mathbb Z$.  For any array, let $Q_p$ truncate each real and
2789	imaginary coefficient part toward zero to this grid.  Then
2790	\begin{equation}
2791	 \|Q_p z-z\|_\infty<\sqrt2\,2^{-p},\qquad
2792	 \|Q_p z\|_\infty\leq\|z\|_\infty.
2793	 \label{eq:transform-truncate}
2794	\end{equation}
2795	
2796	\subsection{Roots, butterflies, and stored frequency order}
2797	
2798	For a power of two $t$ dividing $2r$, define $\omega_t=y^{2r/t}$.
2799	For $z\in\mathcal R_r^t$ and $0\leq j<t$, set
2800	\[
2801	 (F_t^-z)_j=\frac1t\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\omega_t^{-jk}z_k,
2802	 \qquad
2803	 (F_t^+z)_j=\frac1t\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\omega_t^{jk}z_k.
2804	\]
2805	Every power of $\omega_t$ is an isometry, and each transform entry is
2806	an average of $t$ such images.  Thus both transforms are contractions.
2807	The ring has zero divisors, so we verify character cancellation
2808	directly instead of dividing by $\omega_t^j-1$.
2809	
2810	\begin{lemma}[Synthetic character cancellation]
2811	\label{lem:synthetic-characters}
2812	If $j$ is an integer, then
2813	\[
2814	 \sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\omega_t^{jk}
2815	 =\begin{cases}t,&t\mid j,\\0,&t\nmid j.\end{cases}
2816	 \qquad F_t^+F_t^-=t^{-1}I.
2817	\]
2818	\end{lemma}
2819	\begin{proof}
2820	Only the second case needs proof.  Write $j=2^v j_0$ with $j_0$ odd
2821	and $0\leq v<\log_2t$.  Replacing $k$ by $k+t/2^{v+1}$ modulo $t$ permutes
2822	the summands and multiplies their sum by
2823	$y^{rj_0}=-1$.  Hence the sum is zero, since the additive group of
2824	$\mathcal R_r$ has no two-torsion.  Expanding the composite transforms
2825	and applying this identity proves the final formula.
2826	\end{proof}
2827	
2828	Write
2829	\[
2830	 H_0=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
2831	\]
2832	The length-one procedure is the identity.  For $t\geq2$, the
2833	decimation-in-frequency step pairs $z_k$ with $z_{k+t/2}$ for
2834	$0\leq k<t/2$.  The two outputs of $H_0$ occupy these same slots,
2835	whose high address bit is $b=0$ or $b=1$, respectively.  Multiply
2836	the $b=1$ output by $\omega_t^{-k}$, and then apply the length-$t/2$
2837	procedure separately within the two branches.  This computes
2838	$F_t^-$ because, for $b\in\{0,1\}$,
2839	\begin{equation}
2840	 (F_t^-z)_{2h+b}
2841	 =\frac1{t/2}\sum_{k=0}^{t/2-1}
2842	       (\omega_t^2)^{-hk}\omega_t^{-bk}
2843	       \frac{z_k+(-1)^b z_{k+t/2}}2.
2844	 \label{eq:synthetic-dif}
2845	\end{equation}
2846	To follow the recursion, name the original address-bit slots of an
2847	axis of length $t=2^a$ by $a-1,\ldots,0$, from most to least
2848	significant.  For $0\leq s\leq a$, after $s$ levels the values of
2849	the first $s$ named slots are branch bits $b_0,\ldots,b_{s-1}$.
2850	Equation~\eqref{eq:synthetic-dif} identifies these as frequency bits
2851	$0,\ldots,s-1$, numbered from the least significant bit.  The
2852	remaining slots encode an index in $[0,u)$, where $u=t/2^s$.
2853	When $s<a$, the next level uses slot $h=a-1-s$ to distinguish the
2854	paired inputs and then to hold
2855	$b_s$.  Writing $x_v$ for the bit in a still unprocessed slot $v$,
2856	the index used by its twiddle is
2857	\[
2858	       k=\sum_{v=0}^{h-1}2^v x_v,\qquad 0\leq k<u/2.
2859	\]
2860	Previously written branch bits do not enter $k$.  The same description
2861	holds in each shorter branch by \eqref{eq:synthetic-dif}, which proves
2862	the assertion inductively.
2863	
2864	After all $a$ rounds, the named slots from high to low therefore
2865	contain the frequency bits from low to high.  If
2866	$\operatorname{rev}_a(j)$ reverses the $a$ binary digits of $j$, the
2867	entry $(F_t^-z)_j$ occupies slot $\operatorname{rev}_a(j)$.
2868	Let $B_t$ denote this record permutation: it moves the entry at $j$
2869	to $\operatorname{rev}_a(j)$.  The recursion writes its outputs
2870	directly in this order; it does not move whole frequency indices.
2871	
2872	The procedure consuming this stored order traverses the recursion in
2873	reverse: first process the two smaller branches, then apply the inverse
2874	monomial to the second branch, and finally apply $H_0$.  Each forward
2875	level is invertible, since both its butterfly and its monomial are
2876	invertible.  As $H_0^2=I/2$, the reversed level is half the inverse
2877	of the corresponding forward level.  There are $a=\log_2t$ levels,
2878	so the reverse procedure composed with $B_tF_t^-$ is
2879	$2^{-a}I=I/t$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:synthetic-characters} gives the same
2880	composite for $F_t^+B_t^{-1}$ with $B_tF_t^-$.  The forward procedure
2881	is invertible, so these two reverse operators agree.  Thus the two
2882	exact procedures implement
2883	\begin{equation}
2884	       B_tF_t^-,\qquad F_t^+B_t^{-1},
2885	 \label{eq:stored-opposite}
2886	\end{equation}
2887	respectively.

2889	For $D$ axes of lengths $t_1,\ldots,t_D$, put
2890	\[
2891	 M=\prod_{i=1}^D t_i,\qquad
2892	 F_{\boldsymbol t}^\pm=\bigotimes_{i=1}^D F_{t_i}^\pm,
2893	 \qquad B=\bigotimes_{i=1}^D B_{t_i}.
2894	\]
2895	A round applies one current $H_0$ on each participating axis.  The
2896	twiddle for axis $i$ depends only on that axis's address bits.
2897	The two entries paired by another axis's butterfly have the same
2898	axis-$i$ address, so that twiddle commutes with the other butterfly.
2899	Consequently the individual axis steps may be grouped as a parallel
2900	butterfly $\mathcal H$, followed by one recordwise monomial operation
2901	$J_E$.  At each address, $J_E$ multiplies the record by
2902	\begin{equation}
2903	       y^{E},\qquad
2904	 E=-\sum_{i\ \mathrm{participating}}
2905	       \frac{2r}{u_i}\,b_i k_i\pmod{2r}.
2906	 \label{eq:combined-twiddle}
2907	\end{equation}
2908	Here $u_i$ is that axis's current recursive length, $b_i$ its newly
2909	written branch bit, and $0\leq k_i<u_i/2$ is encoded by its still
2910	unprocessed named slots.  The exponent depends on the address, not
2911	on coefficient values.  In the opposite direction the grouped round
2912	is $\mathcal HJ_E^{-1}$: apply $y^{-E}$ first and the parallel
2913	butterfly second.  Each $\mathcal H$ is a contraction and each
2914	$J_E$ is an isometry, so every completed round is a contraction.

2925	cost. The layer then supplies one truncated contraction per round,

3211	To multiply the polynomial records, we use the fixed-tape integer
3212	multiplier of Harvey and van der

3214	$O(N\log(2N))$ on $N$-bit inputs.  This is an independent subroutine.

3216	between coefficient streams and signed integers in the cost. The

3221	\begin{lemma}[Signed packing and normalized ring multiplication]
3222	\label{lem:signed-ring-product}
3223	Let $r=2^\ell<2^p$ with integers $\ell\geq1$ and $p\geq2$, and fix $C_w>1$.
3224	Let $w$ be an integer with $p+2\leq w\leq C_wp$.
3225	The input supplies $\Gamma(p)\Gamma(r)\Gamma(w)$ and two disk grid
3226	polynomials $f,g\in\mathcal R_r$ in the component format of
3227	Proposition~\ref{prop:simultaneous-layer} with width $w$.
3228	One can compute the exact Gaussian integer
3229	numerators of $fg$, and then return $Q_p(fg/r)$ in that same format, in time
3230	$O(rp\log(rp))$ on a fixed number of tapes.  The output is a disk
3231	grid polynomial with error less than $\sqrt2\,2^{-p}$ from $fg/r$.
3232	\end{lemma}
3233	\begin{proof}
3234	The supplied power of two $r$ determines $\ell=\log_2r$.
3235	Write
3236	\[
3237	 f=2^{-p}(a+ib),\qquad g=2^{-p}(c+ie),
3238	\]
3239	where $a,b,c,e\in\mathbb Z[y]$ have degree less than $r$ and
3240	coefficients of absolute value at most $2^p$.  Set $B_0=2^{4p}$
3241	and, for $u\in\{a,b,c,e\}$, define the signed evaluation integer
3242	\[
3243	       A_u=u(B_0)=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}u_jB_0^j.
3244	\]
3245	The bound
3246	\[
3247	 |A_u|\leq2^p\frac{B_0^r-1}{B_0-1}<B_0^r/2
3248	\]
3249	shows that each magnitude fits in $4pr$ bits.  Multiply the four
3250	pairs of absolute values using the established multiplier and restore
3251	each product's sign.  The resulting integers are
3252	$A_aA_c,A_bA_e,A_aA_e,A_bA_c$.  For example, if
3253	$h=ac$ is the ordinary product in $\mathbb Z[y]$, then
3254	\[
3255	       A_aA_c=(ac)(B_0)=\sum_{j=0}^{2r-2}h_jB_0^j.
3256	\]
3257	The other three evaluation products have the same form.  Every
3258	coefficient in any of these ordinary polynomial products satisfies
3259	\begin{equation}
3260	      |h_j|\leq r2^{2p}<2^{3p}<B_0/2.
3261	 \label{eq:packing-separation}
3262	\end{equation}
3263	After the lower coefficients have been removed from an evaluation,
3264	this strict bound identifies the next coefficient by its centered
3265	residue modulo $B_0$.
3266	
3267	To form $A_u$, start with carry $\gamma_0=0$ and write
3268	\[
3269	 d_j\equiv u_j+\gamma_j\pmod{B_0},\quad 0\leq d_j<B_0,
3270	 \qquad \gamma_{j+1}=\frac{u_j+\gamma_j-d_j}{B_0}.
3271	\]
3272	Since $-B_0<u_j+\gamma_j<B_0$ whenever
3273	$\gamma_j\in\{-1,0\}$, the carry stays in $\{-1,0\}$.  Telescoping
3274	the recurrence gives
3275	\[
3276	       A_u=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}d_jB_0^j+\gamma_rB_0^r.
3277	\]
3278	The $r$ blocks are therefore a fixed-width two's-complement encoding
3279	of $A_u$, with $\gamma_r=-1$ exactly when $A_u<0$.  In that case
3280	complement and increment the blocks to obtain $|A_u|$; otherwise
3281	retain them.  Every block has $4p$ bits and every carry has constant
3282	size, so a constant number of scans costs $O(rp)$.  Endianness
3283	changes required by the multiplier are linear-time reversals on a
3284	work tape.
3285	
3286	Now let $Z$ be one of the four signed product integers, and let $h$
3287	be its corresponding ordinary polynomial product.  Put $J=2r$ and
3288	pad that product by $h_{J-1}=0$.  The bound on the evaluation integers
3289	gives $|Z|<B_0^J/4$, so $Z$ fits in $J$ blocks of width $4p$.
3290	Convert its sign and magnitude to sign-extended two's complement:
3291	\[
3292	 Z=\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}q_jB_0^j+\varepsilon B_0^J,
3293	 \qquad 0\leq q_j<B_0,\quad \varepsilon\in\{-1,0\}.
3294	\]
3295	Zero-fill the unused high blocks; for a negative sign, complement
3296	and increment within this fixed width.  These conversions take a
3297	constant number of scans.
3298	Put $\rho_0=0$.  At block $j$, let $\widehat h_j$ be the unique
3299	integer in $[-B_0/2,B_0/2)$ congruent to $q_j+\rho_j$ modulo $B_0$,
3300	and put
3301	\[
3302	       \rho_{j+1}=
3303	          \frac{q_j+\rho_j-\widehat h_j}{B_0}.
3304	\]
3305	The carry belongs to $\{0,1\}$: if $\rho_j$ has this property, then
3306	$0\leq q_j+\rho_j\leq B_0$, and centering either leaves this value
3307	unchanged or subtracts $B_0$.
3308	
3309	The meaning of the carry is the following residual identity, after
3310	coefficients below $j$ have been correctly extracted:
3311	\[
3312	 \sum_{k=j}^{J-1}h_kB_0^{k-j}
3313	 =\sum_{k=j}^{J-1}q_kB_0^{k-j}
3314	       +\rho_j+\varepsilon B_0^{J-j}.
3315	\]
3316	At $j=0$ this is the equality between the two representations of
3317	$Z=h(B_0)$, with
3318	$\rho_0=0$.  For $j<J$, reduction modulo $B_0$ gives
3319	$h_j\equiv q_j+\rho_j\pmod{B_0}$.  By
3320	\eqref{eq:packing-separation}, including the padded value
3321	$h_{J-1}=0$, the unique centered representative is $h_j$ itself.
3322	Thus $\widehat h_j=h_j$.  Subtracting this coefficient and dividing
3323	the residual identity by $B_0$ gives the next identity, with exactly
3324	the displayed update for $\rho_{j+1}$.  At $j=J$ the identity is
3325	$0=\rho_J+\varepsilon$.  Hence a negative product has final carry
3326	$1$, canceled by its sign extension $\varepsilon=-1$; a nonnegative
3327	product has final carry zero.  The machine implements the induction
3328	by reading one block and updating this constant-size carry at each
3329	step, so extraction costs $O(rp)$.
3330	
3331	The real and imaginary numerator streams are respectively
3332	$ac-be$ and $ae+bc$.  To reduce them modulo $y^r+1$, subtract the
3333	coefficient at $j+r$ from the one at $j$ for $0\leq j<r$, treating
3334	a missing coefficient as zero.  Splitting the two halves to tapes
3335	aligns these terms in one further scan.  For each first input index
3336	$j_1\in\{0,\ldots,r-1\}$, exactly one second index $j_2$ in that
3337	range satisfies $j_1+j_2\equiv j\pmod r$.  Its sign is positive
3338	when $j_1+j_2=j$ and negative when $j_1+j_2=j+r$.  Thus each
3339	resulting Gaussian integer coefficient $H_j$ is a sum of exactly
3340	$r$ signed products of Gaussian integer input coefficients of
3341	modulus at most $2^p$.  Consequently
3342	\[
3343	       |H_j|\leq r2^{2p}.
3344	\]
3345	The same triangle inequality before imposing the disk bound gives
3346	$\|fg/r\|_\infty\leq\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_\infty$; in particular the
3347	normalized product of disk polynomials lies in the disk.  All
3348	intermediate coefficient additions fit in $O(p)$ bits.  The
3349	width-$4p$ packing fields and the exact multiplier output prevent
3350	overflow or ambiguity between adjacent fields.
3351	
3352	Finally the $p$-bit grid numerator of the normalized product is
3353	\[
3354	 \operatorname{trunc}_0\left(\frac{\Re H_j}{2^{p+\ell}}\right)
3355	   +i\operatorname{trunc}_0\left(\frac{\Im H_j}{2^{p+\ell}}\right).
3356	\]
3357	To implement it, shift the absolute magnitude right by $p+\ell$
3358	bits and restore its sign, at cost $O(p)$ per coefficient.  The returned
3359	coefficient is $2^{-p}$ times this numerator, namely
3360	$Q_p(2^{-2p}H_j/r)$; \eqref{eq:transform-truncate} proves its error
3361	and disk bounds. Each returned component numerator has magnitude at
3362	most $2^p$, so write it as a signed $w$-bit two's-complement word,
3363	most significant bit first, with the real word before the imaginary
3364	word and coefficient indices in increasing order. This costs
3365	$O(rw)=O(rp)$ and supplies the format used by the opposite transform.
3366	Four exact integer products dominate the linear
3367	packing, extraction, combination, wrapping, and truncation costs.
3368	\end{proof}

3372	For arrays on $\prod_i\mathbb Z/t_i\mathbb Z$ with values in
3373	$\mathcal R_r$, let $*$ denote cyclic convolution in the displayed
3374	axes and define
3375	\[
3376	       \mathcal M_r(f,g)=\frac{f*g}{rM}=\frac{f*g}{T}.
3377	\]

3379	addresses determines one second address, and each of the $r$ first
3380	polynomial indices determines one second index modulo $r$.  The
3381	negacyclic wrap supplies the sign.  Thus that coefficient averages
3382	$rM$ signed scalar products, and $\mathcal M_r$ is a bilinear
3383	contraction:
3384	\[
3385	 \|\mathcal M_r(f,g)\|_\infty
3386	       \leq\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_\infty.
3387	\]
3388	If the other operand is a disk array, replacing one operand changes
3389	the output by at most the norm distance between its two values.

3391	\begin{proposition}[Convolution from the retained transform layout]
3392	\label{prop:synthetic-convolution}

3401	\[
3402	O\left(Tp\left[dK+pK^{\tau-1}+\ell d^{\lambda'}
3403	                    +\log(rp)\right]\right).
3404	\]

3406	original array and coefficient order, with the same two's-complement
3407	component format at width $w_M$. The procedure supplies
3408	$\Gamma(w_M)$ on the output descriptor tape, so the caller knows every
3409	component boundary from this width and the retained shape parameters.

3411	\eqref{eq:synthetic-convolution-error} is at most $1-\rho$, the
3412	returned grid array is a disk array.

3414	\begin{proof}

3435	$\mathcal T_+=F_{\boldsymbol t}^+B^{-1}L^{-1}$.

3437	intact, $P(LBu,LBv)=LBP(u,v)$.  Thus $\mathcal T_+$ applied to the
3438	pointwise product of the exact stored forward outputs equals
3439	$F_{\boldsymbol t}^+P(F_{\boldsymbol t}^-f,F_{\boldsymbol t}^-g)$.
3440	The displayed normalization identity identifies its exact scaling
3441	by $M$ with $\mathcal M_r(f,g)$.
3442	
3443	For the error estimate, put
3444	$\delta=\sqrt2\ell\,2^{-p}$ and $\eta=\sqrt2\,2^{-p}$.
3445	Let $u,v$ be the exact stored forward outputs and
3446	$\widetilde u,\widetilde v$ the returned ones.  All four are disk
3447	arrays, and each forward error is less than $\delta$.
3448	The exact map $P$ is bilinear and satisfies
3449	$\|P(x,y)\|_\infty\leq\|x\|_\infty\|y\|_\infty$ by the coefficient
3450	bound in Lemma~\ref{lem:signed-ring-product}.  Hence
3451	\[
3452	\begin{split}
3453	 P(\widetilde u,\widetilde v)-P(u,v)
3454	   &=P(\widetilde u-u,\widetilde v)+P(u,\widetilde v-v),\\
3455	 \|P(\widetilde u,\widetilde v)-P(u,v)\|_\infty
3456	   &<2\delta,
3457	\end{split}
3458	\]

3460	second uses it on $u$.  Write
3461	$\widetilde z=Q_p(P(\widetilde u,\widetilde v))$ and $z_*=P(u,v)$.

3463	$\|\widetilde z-z_*\|_\infty<2\delta+\eta$.

3465	bound applies to $\widetilde z$.  Since $\mathcal T_+$ is a contraction,
3466	\[
3467	 \|\widetilde h-\mathcal T_+ z_*\|_\infty
3468	 \leq\|\widetilde h-\mathcal T_+\widetilde z\|_\infty
3469	       +\|\mathcal T_+(\widetilde z-z_*)\|_\infty
3470	 <3\delta+\eta.
3471	\]

3473	$M(3\delta+\eta)=\sqrt2\,M(3\ell+1)2^{-p}$, as claimed.
3474	If one original operand has norm at most $\rho$, then
3475	$\|\mathcal M_r(f,g)\|_\infty\leq\rho$.  Under the stated error
3476	margin, the returned norm is less than $\rho+(1-\rho)=1$.

3478	Every computed output before the final scaling is a disk grid array.
3479	The layer's internal dyadic values and the integer product numerators
3480	use the larger exact widths stated in their respective procedures.
3481	The scale $M=2^{m_M}$ is a power of two, so it preserves the $p$-bit
3482	grid. Compute $m_M=\sum_i\log_2t_i$ from the supplied axis lengths.
3483	For each signed $w$-bit numerator returned by the opposite procedure,
3484	append exactly $m_M$ zero bits at its least significant end. This is
3485	the exact two's-complement encoding of the scaled numerator in
3486	$w_M=w+m_M$ bits, including for negative values. The real word still
3487	precedes the imaginary word and the coefficient order is unchanged.
3488	Since $w\leq C_wp$ and $m_M\leq C_\ell p$, this known output width is
3489	$O(p)$. Writing $\Gamma(w_M)$ takes $O(p)$ time.

3491	There are $M=T/r$ pointwise polynomial products.  Their total cost
3492	is $O(Tp\log(rp))$; the three transform costs are as stated, and
3493	the last exact scaling is linear in $Tp$.  All data movement uses
3494	the previously specified scans, swaps, and layout restoration.
3495	\end{proof}
3496	 \section{Resampling with the permutations left in the transform}
3497	\label{sec:resampling}
3498	
3499	The transform lengths needed for the integer product are pairwise coprime,
3500	whereas the synthetic transforms use powers of two. Gaussian resampling
3501	connects these two shapes. Its usual implementation sorts twice on each
3502	coordinate. We retain both permutations in the transform formula and
3503	compute that formula directly. This section proves the resulting interface,
3504	including its tape cost when the number of coordinates grows.
3505	
3506	For an integer $q\geq 1$, write
3507	\[
3508	 (F_q u)_k=\frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}u_j e^{-2\pi i jk/q},
3509	 \qquad
3510	 (F_q^+ u)_k=\frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}u_j e^{2\pi i jk/q}.
3511	\]
3512	All subscripts on a vector of length $q$ are taken modulo $q$.
3513	The vector norm is the maximum modulus of its coordinates. All operator
3514	norms are induced by this norm: $\|L\|=\sup_{\|u\|\leq1}\|Lu\|$.
3515	Each normalized Fourier transform above is a contraction, since each
3516	output averages inputs multiplied by complex numbers of modulus one. Coordinate
3517	permutations preserve the norm.
3518	For an integer precision $p\geq1$, put
3519	\[
3520	 \mathbb D_p=\{2^{-p}(a+ib):a,b\in\mathbb Z,\ a^2+b^2\leq 2^{2p}\}.
3521	\]
3522	For storage between completed scalar routines, put $w_{\rm c}=p+2$.
3523	Represent $2^{-p}(a+ib)\in\mathbb D_p$ by a signed $w_{\rm c}$-bit
3524	two's-complement word for $a$, followed by one for $b$, with each word
3525	written most significant bit first. A coordinate list is the
3526	concatenation of these fixed-length records in its stated order. Since
3527	$|a|,|b|\leq2^p<2^{w_{\rm c}-1}$, this format includes both signs of
3528	every permitted numerator, including $-2^p$ and $2^p$.
3529	An approximation $\widetilde L:\mathbb D_p^a\to\mathbb D_p^b$
3530	to a linear contraction $L:\mathbb C^a\to\mathbb C^b$ has error $E$
3531	if $2^p\|\widetilde L u-Lu\|<E$ for every input in $\mathbb D_p^a$.
3532	The approximation itself need not be linear. Composing such algorithms
3533	adds their errors: at each step, insert the exact map at the computed
3534	input and use its contraction bound on the accumulated input error.
3535	
3536	We use the established $O(N\log N)$ integer multiplier of
3537	Harvey and van der Hoeven~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{HarveyHoeven2021}
3538	for the shorter integer records that occur below. We also use their
3539	Lemma~2.12: for integer precision $p>100$ and integers $k>1$, $0\leq j<k$,
3540	one can compute $\widetilde\zeta\in\mathbb D_p$ with
3541	$2^p|\widetilde\zeta-e^{2\pi i j/k}|<2$ in time
3542	$O(\max(p,\log k)^{1+\delta})$, for every fixed $0<\delta<1/8$.
3543	Throughout this section, numbered citations to that paper refer to its
3544	author-hosted 45-page manuscript.
3545	
3546	\subsection{The one-dimensional interface}
3547	
3548	\begin{lemma}[Resampling without executing the two permutations]
3549	\label{lem:no-sort-resampling}
3550	Fix $0<\delta<1/8$. Let $p>100$, $2\leq s<t<2^p$ and $2\leq\alpha<\sqrt p$
3551	be integers, with $\gcd(s,t)=1$ and
3552	\[
3553	 \theta:=t/s-1>p/\alpha^4.
3554	\]
3555	Define coordinate permutations by
3556	\[
3557	 (P_su)_j=u_{tj},\qquad (P_tv)_k=v_{-sk}.
3558	\]
3559	There are linear contractions $A:\mathbb C^s\to\mathbb C^t$ and
3560	$B_0:\mathbb C^t\to\mathbb C^s$ satisfying
3561	\begin{equation}
3562	 P_sF_s=2^{2\alpha^2}B_0P_tF_tA.
3563	 \label{eq:no-sort-one-dimensional}
3564	\end{equation}
3565	There are fixed multitape algorithms for approximations
3566	$\widetilde A:\mathbb D_p^s\to\mathbb D_p^t$ and
3567	$\widetilde B_0:\mathbb D_p^t\to\mathbb D_p^s$, each with error less
3568	than $p^2$ and time
3569	\[
3570	 O(tp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha).
3571	\]
3572	The constant is uniform in $p,s,t,\alpha$. Inputs and outputs use the
3573	scalar component format above and occur in increasing coordinate order.
3574	\end{lemma}
3575	
3576	\begin{proof}
3577	The Gaussian resampling argument uses two maps
3578	$\mathsf S,\mathsf T:\mathbb C^s\to\mathbb C^t$. For $0\leq k<t$, they are
3579	\[
3580	 (\mathsf S u)_k=\frac1\alpha\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}
3581	 e^{-\pi\alpha^{-2}(j-sk/t)^2}u_j,
3582	 \qquad
3583	 (\mathsf T u)_k=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}
3584	 e^{-\pi\alpha^2(tj/s-k)^2}u_j.
3585	\]
3586	Both sums converge absolutely. For $0\leq j<s$, define
3587	\[
3588	 q_j=\left\lfloor\frac{tj}{s}+\frac12\right\rfloor,
3589	 \qquad \beta_j=\frac{tj}{s}-q_j.
3590	\]
3591	Thus $q_j$ is an integer nearest to $tj/s$, with ties rounded upward.
3592	Let $C:\mathbb C^t\to\mathbb C^s$ select these coordinates, and let
3593	$\mathsf D:\mathbb C^s\to\mathbb C^s$ be the diagonal map
3594	\[
3595	 (Cv)_j=v_{q_j},\qquad
3596	 (\mathsf D u)_j=e^{\pi\alpha^2\beta_j^2}u_j.
3597	\]
3598	Set $N=C\mathsf T\mathsf D$. In $(Nu)_j$, the summand with index $j$
3599	is exactly $u_j$: the factor in $\mathsf D$ cancels the Gaussian factor
3600	at the selected coordinate $q_j$. The other summands form $((N-I)u)_j$.
3601	The exact Gaussian identity and inverse estimate proved in
3602	\cite[Theorem~4.2 and Lemma~4.6]{HarveyHoeven2021} give
3603	\begin{equation}
3604	 \mathsf T P_sF_s=P_tF_t\mathsf S,
3605	 \qquad
3606	 \|N-I\|<2.01e^{-\pi\alpha^2\theta/2}<2^{-\alpha^2\theta}.
3607	 \label{eq:gaussian-public-facts}
3608	\end{equation}
3609	The first identity uses the negative Fourier sign in our definition of
3610	$F_q$; its right-hand permutation is consequently multiplication of the
3611	frequency by $-s$. Since $\alpha^2<p$ and $\theta>p/\alpha^4$, we have
3612	$\alpha^2\theta>p/\alpha^2>1$. Thus $\|N-I\|<1/2$, so $N$ is invertible
3613	by the Neumann series. Put
3614	\[
3615	 \mathsf S'=\mathsf S/2,\qquad
3616	 \mathsf J'=N^{-1}/2,\qquad
3617	 \mathsf D'=2^{-(2\alpha^2-2)}\mathsf D.
3618	\]
3619	The proof of Proposition~4.7(i) in the cited paper gives
3620	\[
3621	 \|\mathsf S'\|<\frac34,\qquad
3622	 \|\mathsf J'\|<\frac78,\qquad
3623	 \|\mathsf D'\|<1.
3624	\]
3625	Now set $A=\mathsf S'$ and $B_0=\mathsf D'\mathsf J'C$.
3626	Because $\|C\|=1$, both are contractions. The diagonal map $\mathsf D$
3627	is invertible, and $C\mathsf T=N\mathsf D^{-1}$, so
3628	\[
3629	 (\mathsf D N^{-1}C)\mathsf T
3630	 =\mathsf D N^{-1}(N\mathsf D^{-1})=I.
3631	\]
3632	Applying this left inverse to the first identity in
3633	\eqref{eq:gaussian-public-facts} gives
3634	$\mathsf D N^{-1}CP_tF_t\mathsf S=P_sF_s$. The normalizations in
3635	$\mathsf D'$, $\mathsf J'$, and $\mathsf S'$ have product
3636	$2^{-(2\alpha^2-2)}2^{-1}2^{-1}=2^{-2\alpha^2}$. Hence
3637	\[
3638	 B_0P_tF_tA
3639	 =2^{-2\alpha^2}\mathsf D N^{-1}CP_tF_t\mathsf S
3640	 =2^{-2\alpha^2}P_sF_s,
3641	\]
3642	which is \eqref{eq:no-sort-one-dimensional}.
3643	
3644	\paragraph{Ordered numerical maps.}
3645	Lemmas~4.8, 4.9 and 4.12 of
3646	\cite{HarveyHoeven2021} supply the following algorithms. Their inputs
3647	and outputs are in increasing coordinate order, and every output is in
3648	the disk grid. The record conversions and tape movement needed to use
3649	these routines in our format are accounted for below. Their numerical
3650	guarantees are
3651	\[
3652	\begin{array}{c|c|c}
3653	 \text{map}&\text{error bound}&\text{time bound}\\ \hline
3654	 \widetilde{\mathsf S}'&16p&O(tp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)\\
3655	 \widetilde{\mathsf J}'&3p^2/4&O(tp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)\\
3656	 \widetilde{\mathsf D}'&4&O(tp^{1+\delta}).
3657	\end{array}
3658	\]
3659	For $C$, observe that $q_0=0$, $q_{s-1}<t$, and $q_{j+1}>q_j$,
3660	because $t/s>1$. Thus $C$ selects an ordered subsequence. A forward scan,
3661	with the current input coordinate stored on a work tape, copies a record
3662	exactly when that coordinate equals the next $q_j$.
3663	
3664	The selected indices can themselves be generated in order using only
3665	$O(p)$ work per index. Precompute $t=hs+\rho$ with $0\leq\rho<s$.
3666	Start with $f_0=e_0=0$, and maintain
3667	$tj=sf_j+e_j$ with $0\leq e_j<s$. At index $j$, first use
3668	$q_j=f_j+\mathbf1_{2e_j\geq s}$. If $j<s-1$, after copying that record
3669	form the values for index $j+1$ by
3670	\[
3671	 c_j=\mathbf1_{e_j+\rho\geq s},\qquad
3672	 e_{j+1}=e_j+\rho-c_js,\qquad
3673	 f_{j+1}=f_j+h+c_j.
3674	\]
3675	Here $e_j+\rho<2s$, so $c_j$ is the only possible carry; the displayed
3676	update gives $t(j+1)=sf_{j+1}+e_{j+1}$. All these counters have $O(p)$
3677	bits. Elementary division computes $h,\rho$ in

3681	Consequently we may take
3682	\[
3683	 \widetilde A=\widetilde{\mathsf S}',
3684	 \qquad
3685	 \widetilde B_0=\widetilde{\mathsf D}'\,
3686	                    \widetilde{\mathsf J}'\,C.
3687	\]
3688	Contraction of the exact maps yields errors less than $16p<p^2$ and
3689	$4+3p^2/4<p^2$, respectively. The costs add to the claimed bound.

3691	The original proof of Proposition~4.7(ii) implements
3692	$B=P_s^{-1}\mathsf D'\mathsf J'CP_t$. Its two label-and-sort operations
3693	implement $P_t$ and $P_s^{-1}$, each costing $O(tp\log t)$.
3694	In \eqref{eq:no-sort-one-dimensional} these permutations remain in the
3695	transform identity. The algorithms for $A$ and $B_0$ use $C$ and the
3696	three quoted arithmetic maps, with all their original truncations.

3698	\paragraph{Record conversion and tape movement.}
3699	We specify how these scalar records meet the cited numerical interfaces.
3700	Sections~2.1--2.2 of the cited paper use standard binary integers, represent
3701	$2^{-p}(a+ib)\in\mathbb D_p$ by the exact integer pair $(a,b)$ with $p$
3702	known, and store vectors as ordered coordinate lists. The cited
3703	exponential and Gaussian routines return grid values in this
3704	representation. Their computed numerator pairs are exact representations
3705	of the approximations; the numerical errors remain those stated for the
3706	approximated analytic maps. The source leaves the sign code, digit order,
3707	padding and field boundaries open, so we make a concrete choice when
3708	implementing its constructive algorithms.
3709	
3710	At each scalar input or output boundary of a cited routine, use one sign
3711	symbol, the ordinary binary magnitude in most-significant-bit-first order,
3712	and a fixed separator for
3713	each integer. Use one zero digit and the nonnegative sign for zero, put
3714	the real field before the imaginary field, and concatenate pairs in
3715	coordinate order. Each grid numerator magnitude has at most $p+1$ digits.
3716	To convert one field to our $w_{\rm c}$-bit word, buffer its magnitude, right-align
3717	it in a zero-filled block of that width, and, for a negative sign,
3718	complement the block and add one from right to left. Copy the block from
3719	left to right to the output. The inverse conversion reads one complete
3720	$w_{\rm c}$-bit word, remembers its leading sign, complements and adds
3721	one if negative, and emits the signed magnitude after removing leading
3722	zeroes. In both directions the represented integer is unchanged.
3723	
3724	A unary ruler of $w_{\rm c}$ cells is prepared once per call by starting
3725	with an empty ruler and reading the binary digits of $p$ from most to least
3726	significant, successively doubling the current unary prefix
3727	and appending one cell when the next digit is one, then adding two cells.
3728	This takes $O(p)$ time. Reusing the ruler, a constant
3729	number of sweeps of the current field and work blocks performs each
3730	conversion, including head returns and cleanup, in $O(p)$ time on fixed
3731	tapes. Separators identify the next source field, and the ruler identifies
3732	the next fixed-width word; the input head finishes after the consumed
3733	field and the output head after the appended field. The inverse adapter
3734	supplies the Gaussian input vectors, and the forward adapter formats their
3735	outputs. Lemma~2.12 instead receives the ordinary binary integers $j,k$
3736	and needs only the output adapter. These value-preserving conversions add
3737	no error. On the Gaussian line lengths $s<t$, their
3738	$O((s+t)p)=O(tp)$ work, and their $O(p)$ work per exponential output,
3739	are included in the stated bounds.
3740	
3741	The remaining tape movement inside the quoted algorithms also has the
3742	claimed bound. The $\mathsf S'$ procedure uses a consecutive periodic input
3743	window of radius $\lceil\sqrt p\rceil\alpha$ for each output. Visiting
3744	these $O(p)$-bit records costs $O(tp\sqrt p\alpha)$ tape steps.
3745	Remark~4.10 in the cited paper charges the extra jumps at the cyclic
3746	boundary by the same bound.
3747	
3748	The Neumann evaluation also keeps its computed records bounded.
3749	Put $E=N-I$ and $k=\lceil p/(\alpha^2\theta)\rceil$. Under the present
3750	hypotheses, Lemma~4.11 gives, for every $z\in\mathbb D_p^s$,
3751	\[
3752	 \widetilde E z\in\mathbb D_p^s,\qquad
3753	 2^p\|\widetilde E z-Ez\|<p/3.
3754	\]
