3794	\subsection{Growing dimension and the padded array}
3795	
3796	For the tensor product, apply the one-dimensional maps to one coordinate
3797	line at a time. The chunk-swap algorithm supplies the movement of the
3798	physical axis fields, including its cost when the number of axes grows.
3799	
3800	\begin{lemma}[Tensor interface]
3801	\label{lem:tensor-resampling}
3802	Suppose every pair $(s_i,t_i)$, $1\leq i\leq d$, satisfies
3803	Lemma~\ref{lem:no-sort-resampling} with the same $p,\alpha,\delta$.
3804	Put $T=\prod_i t_i$, $\gamma=2d\alpha^2$, and
3805	\[
3806	 R=\bigotimes_iP_{s_i},\quad Q=\bigotimes_iP_{t_i},\quad
3807	 \mathcal A=\bigotimes_i A_i,\quad
3808	 \mathcal B_0=\bigotimes_i B_{0,i}.
3809	\]
3810	Then
3811	\begin{equation}
3812	 RF_{\boldsymbol s}
3813	   =2^\gamma\mathcal B_0QF_{\boldsymbol t}\mathcal A,
3814	 \qquad F_{\boldsymbol q}:=\bigotimes_iF_{q_i}.
3815	 \label{eq:no-sort-tensor}
3816	\end{equation}
3817	Also write $F_{\boldsymbol q}^+=\bigotimes_iF_{q_i}^+$.
3818	Both $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B_0$ are contractions. The linewise
3819	implementations of $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B_0$ each have error
3820	less than $dp^2$. The total time spent in the
3821	one-dimensional algorithms for both maps is
3822	$O(dTp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)$, with a constant independent of $d$.
3823	
3824	If each $t_i\in\{r/2,r\}$ with $r=2^\ell$, the array is kept in the
3825	full padded box of $T$ entries, and each entry occupies $O(p)$ bits,
3826	then exposing and restoring all the lines costs
3827	\[
3828	 O\bigl(Tp\,d^2(1+\ell^\tau)\bigr)
3829	\]
3830	using the equal-width chunk-swap bound $O(Vu^\tau)$ and the fixed-digit
3831	movement primitive. Any fixed polynomial in $p$ of setup per line is
3832	negligible compared with $Tp$ when $r$ grows faster than every such
3833	polynomial and $d$ is polynomially bounded in $p$.
3834	\end{lemma}
3835	
3836	\begin{proof}
3837	Tensoring \eqref{eq:no-sort-one-dimensional} proves
3838	\eqref{eq:no-sort-tensor}. To implement $\mathcal A$, first embed its
3839	input in the padded box by writing zero outside
3840	$\prod_i[0,s_i)$. Expand the axes one at a time. After the axes in a set
3841	$I$ have been expanded, the valid entries have coordinate ranges
3842	$[0,t_i)$ for $i\in I$ and $[0,s_i)$ otherwise; every other entry is
3843	zero. Expose the next axis $i$ as the innermost address field. On a line
3844	whose other coordinates are valid, read its first $s_i$ values and apply
3845	$\widetilde A_i$, then write the resulting $t_i$ values. On every other
3846	line write $t_i$ zeros. The new valid set is the one for $I\cup\{i\}$.
3847	
3848	For compression, start with all coordinates in $[0,t_i)$ valid.
3849	After a set $J$ of axes has been compressed, validity means
3850	$j_h<s_h$ for $h\in J$ and $j_h<t_h$ otherwise. For the next axis $i$,
3851	apply $\widetilde B_{0,i}$ to each $t_i$-line whose other coordinates
3852	are valid. Write its $s_i$ outputs followed by $t_i-s_i$ zeros.
3853	A line invalid on another coordinate is already zero; consume it and
3854	write a zero line without calling $\widetilde B_{0,i}$. The box therefore
3855	keeps its full size, and the new valid set is the one for $J\cup\{i\}$.
3856	
3857	For a fixed axis, the exact map acts independently on its valid lines
3858	and is zero on the other lines. Taking the maximum over the line norms
3859	shows that this axis map is a contraction; taking the maximum of the
3860	line errors gives an error less than $p^2$ for the whole axis.
3861	Composing the $d$ axis maps gives error less than $dp^2$.
3862	At most $T/t_i$ lines invoke the one-dimensional algorithm for axis $i$,
3863	so their cost is bounded by
3864	\[
3865	 \sum_{i=1}^d\frac{T}{t_i}
3866	           O(t_i p^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)
3867	   =O(dTp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha).
3868	\]
3869	Initial padding costs $O(Tp)$, and scanning and zeroing the remaining
3870	lines costs $O(Tp)$ per axis. Both are within the same bound.
3871	All calls reuse one fixed collection of work
3872	tapes. Loop indices and the growing shape descriptor reside on tapes;
3873	they are not extra heads.
3874	
3875	The descriptor records which coordinate each physical address field
3876	holds. Thus moving fields changes their positions, but not the validity
3877	conditions above. To move an axis past its neighbor, interchange their
3878	$\ell$-bit or $(\ell-1)$-bit address fields. Equal widths use
3879	Lemma~\ref{lem:chunk-swap}. For unequal widths, write the longer field as
3880	a leading bit $e$ followed by $\ell-1$ bits. If it comes first, the order
3881	is $e\,x\,y$, with $x,y$ of equal width. Interchange $x,y$, then move $e$
3882	between them, obtaining $y\,e\,x$. If the longer field comes second,
3883	first move its leading bit left of the shorter field, then interchange
3884	the two equal-width pieces. The bit move uses
3885	Lemma~\ref{lem:elementary-streams}. Each adjacent interchange therefore
3886	costs $O(Tp(1+\ell^\tau))$. Exposing and restoring one axis needs
3887	$O(d)$ adjacent interchanges, hence all axes need $O(d^2)$. These are
3888	exact permutations of the padded box, so they change neither norms nor
3889	errors.
3890	
3891	Since $t_i\geq r/2$, each tensor map invokes at most
3892	$\sum_iT/t_i\leq2dT/r$ lines. For any fixed setup degree $c$, work
3893	$O(p^c)$ per line totals $O(dTp^c/r)=o(Tp)$: after division by $Tp$,
3894	the ratio is $O(dp^{c-1}/r)$, which tends to zero under the stated growth
3895	assumptions. This estimate includes local descriptor copying, validity
3896	tests per line, and preparing line boundaries.
3897	\end{proof}

3899	\subsection{The middle transform and the final permutation}
3900	
3901	The factor $QF_{\boldsymbol t}$ in \eqref{eq:no-sort-tensor} can be
3902	computed from a cyclic convolution and two pointwise phase
3903	multiplications. The chirp identity below performs the frequency change
3904	in $Q$ without applying $Q$ as a separate permutation of the array.
3905	The second identity shows how the
3906	retained source permutation $R$ cancels when computing a convolution.
3907	Here $*$ denotes
3908	cyclic convolution on the product of the coordinate groups and a dot
3909	denotes coordinatewise multiplication.
3910	
3911	\begin{lemma}[Chirp and permutation cancellation]
3912	\label{lem:chirp-permutation}
3913	With $R,Q,s_i,t_i$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:tensor-resampling},
3914	assume every $t_i$ is even. For $\boldsymbol j\in\mathbb Z^d$, define
3915	\[
3916	 a_{\boldsymbol j}
3917	 =\exp\left(-\pi i\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{s_i j_i^2}{t_i}\right).
3918	\]
3919	Then $a$ has period $t_i$ in coordinate $i$, and
3920	\begin{equation}
3921	 QF_{\boldsymbol t}u
3922	 =\overline a\mathbin{\cdot}
3923	       \frac{a*(\overline a\mathbin{\cdot}u)}{T}.
3924	 \label{eq:permuted-chirp}
3925	\end{equation}
3926	If $S=\prod_i s_i$, then
3927	\begin{equation}
3928	 (RF_{\boldsymbol s}^+)
3929	   \bigl[(RF_{\boldsymbol s}u)\mathbin{\cdot}
3930	         (RF_{\boldsymbol s}v)\bigr]
3931	 =\frac{u*v}{S^2}.
3932	 \label{eq:source-permutation-cancel}
3933	\end{equation}
3934	Complex conjugation of the input and output of an algorithm for
3935	$RF_{\boldsymbol s}$ gives an algorithm for $RF_{\boldsymbol s}^+$.
3936	\end{lemma}
3937	
3938	\begin{proof}
3939	Replacing $j_i$ by $j_i+t_i$ changes the exponent defining $a$ by
3940	$-\pi i s_i(2j_i+t_i)$, an integral multiple of $2\pi i$.
3941	The coefficient of $u_{\boldsymbol k}$ in the right side of
3942	\eqref{eq:permuted-chirp} is
3943	\[
3944	 \frac1T\overline a_{\boldsymbol j}
3945	               a_{\boldsymbol j-\boldsymbol k}
3946	               \overline a_{\boldsymbol k}
3947	 =\frac1T\exp\left(2\pi i\sum_i
3948	                       \frac{s_i j_i k_i}{t_i}\right).
3949	\]
3950	This is precisely the coefficient in $QF_{\boldsymbol t}$, because
3951	$Q$ reads frequency $(-s_i j_i)_i$ from the negative-sign transform.
3952	
3953	For a unit $c$ modulo $q$, let $(R_cz)_j=z_{cj}$. Substituting $h=ck$
3954	in the Fourier sum gives
3955	\[
3956	 (F_q^+R_cz)_j
3957	 =\frac1q\sum_{h=0}^{q-1}z_h e^{2\pi i h c^{-1}j/q}
3958	 =(R_c^{-1}F_q^+z)_j.
3959	\]
3960	Each $t_i$ is a unit modulo $s_i$, so tensoring this identity gives
3961	$F_{\boldsymbol s}^+R=R^{-1}F_{\boldsymbol s}^+$ and hence
3962	$RF_{\boldsymbol s}^+R=F_{\boldsymbol s}^+$. Also
3963	$(RF_{\boldsymbol s}u)\mathbin{\cdot}(RF_{\boldsymbol s}v)
3964	=R(F_{\boldsymbol s}u\mathbin{\cdot}F_{\boldsymbol s}v)$,
3965	because a coordinate permutation commutes with pointwise products.
3966	Therefore
3967	\[
3968	 RF_{\boldsymbol s}^+\bigl[R(F_{\boldsymbol s}u\mathbin{\cdot}
3969	                                       F_{\boldsymbol s}v)\bigr]
3970	 =F_{\boldsymbol s}^+(F_{\boldsymbol s}u\mathbin{\cdot}
3971	                                       F_{\boldsymbol s}v).
3972	\]
3973	The normalized convolution rule is
3974	$F_{\boldsymbol s}(u*v)=S(F_{\boldsymbol s}u)\mathbin{\cdot}
3975	(F_{\boldsymbol s}v)$, while
3976	$F_{\boldsymbol s}^+F_{\boldsymbol s}=I/S$. The two normalizations give
3977	\[
3978	 F_{\boldsymbol s}^+
3979	   (F_{\boldsymbol s}u\mathbin{\cdot}F_{\boldsymbol s}v)
3980	 =\frac1S F_{\boldsymbol s}^+F_{\boldsymbol s}(u*v)
3981	 =\frac{u*v}{S^2},
3982	\]
3983	proving \eqref{eq:source-permutation-cancel}. Finally, conjugation
3984	changes the negative Fourier sign to the positive one and commutes with
3985	the real permutation $R$. It preserves both the disk grid and the norm,
3986	so conjugating the input and output also preserves an algorithm's error
3987	bound.
3988	\end{proof}
3989	 \section{Exact integer multiplication and its cost}
3990	\label{sec:assembly}
3991	
3992	We now use the preceding algorithms to multiply two $n$-bit integers.
3993	An equal-width address swap on logical bit volume $V$ costs
3994	$O(Vu^\tau)$ for width $u$.  A completed parallel normalized butterfly
3995	layer costs $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ and has coefficient error less than
3996	$\sqrt2\,2^{-p}$.  The ordered Gaussian resampling maps are
3997	contractions; their disk-grid approximations have error less than
3998	$p^2 2^{-p}$ and cost $O(tp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)$ on a line of length
3999	$t$.  Address permutations and intermediate dyadic arithmetic are
4000	exact.  We choose compatible parameters for these procedures, recover
4001	the integer coefficients from their approximations, and account for the
4002	remaining tape operations.
4003	
4004	\subsection{A fixed rational choice}
4005	
4006	The two motif exponents were fixed in \eqref{eq:explicit-motif-exponents}.
4007	Take the following fixed rational numbers:
4008	\begin{equation}\label{eq:fixed-parameters}
4009	\begin{gathered}
4010	 \tau=\sigma=1-2^{-50},\qquad \beta=\frac12,\qquad \delta=\frac1{16},\\
4011	 \lambda=1-2^{-52},\qquad c=2^{-56},\qquad

4019	\[
4020	 \max\{\tau,\sigma\}<\lambda<1,\qquad
4021	 \tau(1+c/\beta)<1-31\cdot2^{-55}<\lambda,

4023	and
4024	\[
4025	 \sigma+\beta(1-\sigma)=1-2^{-51}<\lambda<\lambda'<1.
4026	\]

4028	a base-$m$ partition.  The dimension exponent also satisfies
4029	\[
4030	\begin{gathered}
4031	 \epsilon<\frac1{12},\quad \epsilon C_1<1,\quad
4032	 \epsilon(2-\tau)<1-\tau,\quad
4033	 \frac34+\delta+\frac32\epsilon<1,\\

4038	\subsection{Input and transform sizes}
4039	
4040	The input is the promised string $x\#y$, with both operands written
4041	most significant bit first.  In one left-to-right pass, copy $x$ and
4042	$y$ to two fixed work tapes and count the bits of $x$ with a binary
4043	counter.  The promise gives both operands this counted length $n$.
4044	The counter bound in Section~\ref{sec:streams} and the two sequential
4045	copies give cost $O(n)$, including all leading zeroes.  The work-copy
4046	heads finish just after the least significant bits, ready to move
4047	leftward when the digits are formed.
4048	
4049	\subsubsection{The padded box and working precision}
4050	
4051	After obtaining $n$, compute the size parameters below with the
4052	separate setup costs stated in this subsection.  For sufficiently
4053	large $n$, put
4054	\[
4055	 b=\lceil\log_2n\rceil,\quad p=6b,\quad d=\lfloor b^\epsilon\rfloor,
4056	 \quad K=\lfloor d^c\rfloor.
4057	\]
4058	Take the power of two $T$ in $[4n/b,8n/b)$, and let
4059	$r=2^{\lceil(\log_2T)/d\rceil}$ and $\ell=\log_2r$.  Choose
4060	$d\ell-\log_2T$ of the $d$ axis lengths to be $r/2$ and the others to
4061	be $r$.  This gives
4062	\[
4063	 t_i\in\{r/2,r\},\qquad \prod_i t_i=T,\qquad t_d=r.
4064	\]
4065	Indeed $d\ell-\log_2T$ is an integer in $[0,d)$, so at least one axis
4066	has length $r$; choose it as the last axis.
4067	These definitions give
4068	\begin{equation}\label{eq:sizes}
4069	 Tp=\Theta(n),\quad d=\Theta(p^\epsilon),\quad
4070	 K=\Theta(p^{\epsilon c}),\quad
4071	 \ell=\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon}),\quad r=2^{\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon})}.
4072	\end{equation}
4073	The comparison constants can be fixed for every input length at once.
4074	For sufficiently large $b$, the bounds on $n,T$ give
4075	$b/2\leq\log_2T\leq b$. Since $p=6b$, $d=\lfloor b^\epsilon\rfloor$
4076	and $d\leq b$, they imply
4077	\[
4078	 \frac1{12}p^\epsilon\leq d\leq p^\epsilon,
4079	 \qquad \frac{p}{12d}\leq\ell\leq\frac{p}{3d}.
4080	\]
4081	Thus we fix $a_d=a_r=1/12$, $b_d=1$, $b_r=1/3$, and $C_\ell=1$
4082	in the layer and transform interfaces. Their pointwise bounds cover every
4083	computed pair $(d,r)$, including all choices arising at the same $p$.
4084	These bounds also give that $r$ exceeds every fixed power of $p$,
4085	$K/\log p\to\infty$, and
4086	$\ell/K\to\infty$.  There are eventually enough axes for the
4087	$O(\log d)$ reserved row axes and enough bits for all work blocks.
4088	
4089	Set
4090	\[
4091	 \alpha=\left\lceil(12d^2b)^{1/4}\right\rceil,
4092	 \qquad \gamma=2d\alpha^2,\qquad \eta=\frac1{4d}.
4093	\]
4094	The ceiling does not affect the needed bounds: for $A\ge1$,
4095	$\lceil A\rceil\le2A$, and hence
4096	\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma}
4097	 \alpha\le2(12d^2b)^{1/4},\qquad
4098	 \gamma<28d^2\sqrt b\le28b^{1/2+2\epsilon}\le28b^{2/3}.
4099	\end{equation}
4100	It follows that $2\le\alpha<\sqrt p$ eventually and $\gamma=o(b)$.
4101	For example $b\ge2^{24}$ implies $\gamma\le b/4$.
4102	
4103	\subsubsection{Prime source lengths}
4104	
4105	The distinct prime lengths $s_i$ must be close to the powers of two
4106	$t_i$: their product must occupy a fixed fraction of the padded box,
4107	while each ratio $t_i/s_i$ must leave enough separation for resampling.
4108	We verify both requirements for the parameters just chosen.
4109	
4110	The prime-interval result
4111	\cite[Lemma~5.1]{HarveyHoeven2021}, based on explicit estimates of
4112	Rosser and Schoenfeld~\cite{RosserSchoenfeld1962}, gives the following
4113	bound: for
4114	$0<\eta<1/4$ and $x>e^{2/\eta}$, the interval
4115	\[
4116	 (1-2\eta)x<q\leq(1-\eta)x
4117	\]
4118	contains at least $\eta x/(2\log x)$ primes. Here $\log$ is the natural
4119	logarithm. The size bounds in \eqref{eq:sizes} give
4120	$d=\Theta(p^\epsilon)$ and $\log r=\Theta(p/d)$.
4121	For large $n$ we have $d\geq2$, so
4122	$0<\eta<1/4$, and
4123	\[
4124	 \frac{\log(r/2)}d=\Theta(p^{1-2\epsilon})\longrightarrow\infty.
4125	\]
4126	Thus both $x=r/2$ and $x=r$ satisfy $\log x>8d=2/\eta$.
4127	For either choice, the stated lower bound for the number of primes is
4128	$x/(8d\log x)$ and exceeds $d$:
4129	indeed, $\log x=\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon})$, whereas
4130	$\log(8d^2\log x)=O(\log p)=o(\log x)$, so $x>8d^2\log x$ eventually.
4131	The two intervals are disjoint because
4132	$(1-\eta)r/2<(1-2\eta)r$ for $\eta<1/4$, and both intervals lie above
4133	$2$. We may therefore choose distinct odd primes satisfying
4134	\[
4135	 (1-2\eta)t_i<s_i\leq(1-\eta)t_i.
4136	\]
4137	Every $\gcd(s_i,t_i)$ equals one because $t_i$ is a power of two.
4138	Put $S=\prod_i s_i$. Multiplying the lower bounds on $s_i$ and
4139	applying strict Bernoulli inequality gives
4140	\[
4141	 \frac ST>
4142	 \left(1-\frac1{2d}\right)^d>\frac12
4143	 \qquad(d\geq2).
4144	\]
4145	Together with $s_i<t_i$, this gives $T/2<S<T$.
4146	Writing $\theta_i=t_i/s_i-1$, the upper bound on $s_i$ gives
4147	$\theta_i\geq\eta/(1-\eta)>\eta$. Therefore
4148	\[
4149	 \alpha^4\theta_i>\frac{12d^2b}{4d}=3db\geq6b=p.
4150	\]
4151	The choice of $\alpha$ gives
4152	$\alpha=\Theta(p^{1/4+\epsilon/2})$, and \eqref{eq:gamma} already
4153	ensures $2\leq\alpha<\sqrt p$ for large $n$. We also have
4154	$t_i\leq r\leq T<8n/b<2^{6b}=2^p$.
4155	Thus every hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:no-sort-resampling} holds for
4156	all sufficiently large input lengths. The superpolynomial growth of $r$
4157	established above also supplies the setup condition in
4158	Lemma~\ref{lem:tensor-resampling}.
4159	
4160	The machine finds these primes by scanning the two intervals
4161	deterministically and testing each candidate by trial division through
4162	its square root. Testing every candidate would visit $O(r)$ candidates
4163	and at most $O(\sqrt r)$ trial divisors per candidate. Elementary
4164	division on $O(\log r)$-bit integers and management of a list of at most
4165	$d$ selected primes give the conservative bound
4166	$O(dr^{3/2}\operatorname{poly}(p))$. Its logarithm is
4167	\[
4168	 O(\log p+\log r)=O(\log p+p/d)=o(p).
4169	\]
4170	Since $p=6\lceil\log_2 n\rceil=\Theta(\log n)$, the search takes
4171	$n^{o(1)}=o(n)$ time.
4172	All remaining scalar setup, including comparisons for fixed rational
4173	powers, modular inverses,
4174	prime products and shape descriptors, has cost polynomial in $p$.
4175	For example, $d=\lfloor b^{2^{-75}}\rfloor$ is found by binary search
4176	using exact comparisons $d^{2^{75}}\le b$; the exponent is fixed.
4177	The same procedure computes $K$ and all other fixed rational powers.
4178	All primes and length parameters are therefore generated by the machine;
4179	they are not advice.

4181	\subsubsection{The radix-digit polynomials}
4182	
4183	Write the two inputs as polynomials in $2^b$, each with
4184	$q=\lceil n/b\rceil$ nonnegative digits.  Their product has degree at most
4185	\[
4186	 2q-2<2n/b\le T/2<S.
4187	\]
4188	Thus convolution modulo $x^S-1$ has no nonzero wraparound.  Every product
4189	coefficient obeys
4190	\begin{equation}\label{eq:capacity}
4191	 0\le c_j\le q(2^b-1)^2<2^{3b},
4192	\end{equation}
4193	since $q\le n\le2^b$.

4195	\subsection{An explicit cyclic-convolution layout}
4196	
4197	To use the source tensor, we first place the ordinary coefficient stream
4198	in its tensor order. Agarwal and Cooley used the Chinese remainder
4199	theorem to convert one cyclic convolution into multidimensional cyclic
4200	convolution~\cite{AgarwalCooley1977}. The following map uses that
4201	algebraic split, with coordinate powers that make the change of order a
4202	sequence of controlled cyclic shifts.
4203	
4204	Let $s_1,\ldots,s_d$ be the pairwise coprime
4205	source lengths, let $S=\prod_i s_i$, and put
4206	\[
4207	 P_i=\prod_{j<i}s_j,\qquad \mu_i=P_i^{-1}\pmod{s_i}.
4208	\]
4209	Here $P_i$ denotes an integer prefix product, not a Fourier-coordinate
4210	permutation.  The assignment
4211	\[
4212	 \Phi:\mathbb C[x]/(x^S-1)\longrightarrow
4213	 \mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_d]/(x_1^{s_1}-1,\ldots,x_d^{s_d}-1),
4214	 \qquad x\longmapsto\prod_i x_i^{\mu_i}
4215	\]
4216	respects $x^S=1$, so it defines an algebra map.  The target monomial
4217	group has size $S$, and the image of $x$ has order $S$, because each
4218	$\mu_i$ is a unit and the $s_i$ are pairwise coprime.  Its powers
4219	therefore run through all target basis monomials exactly once.  Hence
4220	$\Phi$ is an isomorphism and preserves cyclic convolution.
4221	
4222	Every ordinary coefficient index has a unique mixed-radix expression
4223	\[
4224	 k=\sum_{j=1}^d a_jP_j,\qquad 0\le a_j<s_j.
4225	\]
4226	The coordinate of $\Phi(x^k)$ in axis $i$ is
4227	\begin{equation}\label{eq:triangular-crt}
4228	 b_i=a_i+\mu_i\sum_{j<i}a_jP_j\pmod{s_i}.
4229	\end{equation}
4230	Indeed terms with $j>i$ are divisible by $s_i$, and $\mu_iP_i=1$ modulo
4231	$s_i$.  Numerical order of $k$ is lexicographic order of
4232	$(a_d,\ldots,a_1)$.  Insert the padding in one nested scan of the full
4233	box $\prod_i[0,t_i)$ in this lexicographic order, with $a_d$ the
4234	outermost counter and $a_1$ the innermost.  At an address satisfying
4235	$a_i<s_i$ for every $i$, copy the next original coefficient record;
4236	at every other address, write a zero record.  The valid addresses
4237	occur in the original coefficient order, so each record is copied to
4238	its intended mixed-radix address.  To delete the padding after the
4239	inverse axis reorder, use the same enumeration, copying the record at
4240	each valid address and skipping the record at each invalid address.
4241	
4242	Store the nested binary counters consecutively on a fixed work tape.
4243	Their total width is $\sum_i\log_2t_i=\log_2T=O(p)$, and the stored
4244	bounds $s_i$ also have total width $O(p)$.  At each of the $T$
4245	addresses, updating the counters, testing validity, and handling the
4246	$O(p)$-bit record therefore cost $O(p)$ steps, including counter-head
4247	returns.  Each insertion or deletion scan costs $O(Tp)$.
4248	
4249	Now reorder the complete padded axes to $(a_1,\ldots,a_d)$.  In this
4250	physical order, the coordinates with
4251	indices below $i$ precede coordinate $i$.  Update the targets in the
4252	order $i=d,d-1,\ldots,1$ using \eqref{eq:triangular-crt}.  When target
4253	$i$ is updated, none of its lower-index controls has yet changed, so
4254	the offset is computed from the original digits $a_j$ required by the
4255	formula.
4256	
4257	To specify the action on padded addresses, let
4258	\[
4259	 \mathcal P=\prod_i[0,t_i),\qquad \mathcal V=\prod_i[0,s_i)
4260	\]
4261	be sets of integer addresses.  On a fixed control prefix, rotate the
4262	valid target interval $[0,s_i)$ by the offset in
4263	\eqref{eq:triangular-crt} and fix $[s_i,t_i)$.  If any lower-index
4264	control is invalid, use the identity.  This defines a bijection of
4265	$\mathcal P$: for fixed controls and spectators it is a cyclic
4266	permutation of the valid target interval and the identity elsewhere.
4267	Each step preserves $\mathcal V$ and its complement.  Consequently
4268	zero padding remains zero after every step.  An inverse is explicit:
4269	process $i=1,\ldots,d$, subtracting the same expression formed from the
4270	already recovered lower coordinates; then undo the axis reorder and
4271	perform the deletion scan just described.
4272	
4273	Each triangular update is a prefix-controlled cyclic shift.  The
4274	controls precede its target in the current physical order.  For each
4275	prefix, prepare the offset, split the valid target interval into its
4276	two consecutive pieces, and merge those pieces in the opposite order.
4277	Every target position carries its full spectator suffix as a block;
4278	the invalid interval is copied unchanged.  There are at most $T/t_i$
4279	control prefixes for target $i$.  For any fixed setup degree $C$, all
4280	offsets therefore cost $O(dTp^C/r)=o(Tp)$ to prepare, since
4281	$t_i\ge r/2$ and $r$ exceeds every fixed power of $p$.
4282	
4283	The axis widths are $\ell$ or $\ell-1$.  To exchange two adjacent axes
4284	of unequal width, move the longer axis's leading bit outside their
4285	equal-width pair, swap that pair by the proved chunk-swap procedure,
4286	and put the leading bit at its new position.  This adds a fixed number
4287	of linear passes to the equal-width swap cost.  Reversing all axes
4288	uses $O(d^2)$ such moves.  Therefore the map $\Phi$, its inverse, and
4289	their padding operations cost
4290	\[
4291	 O\bigl(Tp\,d^2(1+\ell^\tau)\bigr).
4292	\]
4293	This construction describes payload movement from address $a$ to its
4294	new address.  It is distinct from the operator convention
4295	$(R_cz)_j=z_{cj}$ used for Fourier dilations, which moves a payload
4296	from address $j$ to $c^{-1}j$.
4297	
4298	\subsection{Complex convolution by a coefficient twist}
4299

4300	The power-of-two complex convolution used in the chirp identity is
4301	obtained from the synthetic convolution by a coefficient twist.
4302	Put $\mathcal R=\mathcal R_r=\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$ and
4303	$\zeta=e^{\pi i/r}$.  The map
4304	\[
4305	 \Theta:\mathbb C[x_d]/(x_d^r-1)\longrightarrow\mathcal R,
4306	 \qquad x_d\longmapsto\zeta y
4307	\]
4308	is well defined, since $(\zeta y)^r=(-1)(-1)=1$.  On the bases
4309	$(x_d^k)_{0\le k<r}$ and $(y^k)_{0\le k<r}$ it is diagonal,
4310	multiplying coefficient $k$ by the nonzero number $\zeta^k$.  It is therefore an
4311	isomorphism, with inverse multiplying that coefficient by
4312	$\zeta^{-k}$.  Both exact maps preserve the coefficient sup norm.
4313	For an explicit check on the wrap, write $k+l=j+hr$, where
4314	$h\in\{0,1\}$.  A product term after twisting and negacyclic reduction
4315	has factor
4316	\[
4317	 \zeta^{k+l}(-1)^h=\zeta^j(\zeta^r)^h(-1)^h=\zeta^j.
4318	\]
4319	Untwisting therefore recovers the cyclic coefficient with the correct
4320	sign.  We next specify how this linewise map meets the ring-convolution
4321	interface.  Put $M=\prod_{i<d}t_i=T/r$.  For a complex array $f$ on
4322	$\prod_{i=1}^d\mathbb Z/t_i\mathbb Z$, with $t_d=r$, define
4323	\[
4324	 (\iota f)_{\boldsymbol j}
4325	   =\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}f_{\boldsymbol j,k}y^k,
4326	 \qquad
4327	 \boldsymbol j\in\prod_{i<d}\mathbb Z/t_i\mathbb Z.
4328	\]

4488	The source-transform procedures now supply the three transforms needed
4489	for the radix-digit convolution. Read each stored operand backward from

4492	group on a fixed work tape and read it back most significant bit first,
4493	reversing its least-significant-first input order; pad the final short
4494	group with leading zeroes.

4496	$a_j2^{p-b-2}$ in a signed $w_{\rm c}$-bit real word, followed by a zero
4497	$w_{\rm c}$-bit imaginary word. This exponent is nonnegative
4498	because $p=6b$, and the represented value is exactly $a_j2^{-b-2}$.
4499	Append $S-q$ zero coefficient records.  Buffering and ordering the
4500	groups costs $O(n)$, including the one partial group's padding, and
4501	writing the $S$ records costs $O(Sp)$.
4502	Together with the initial count and copies, this input conversion
4503	costs $O(n+Sp)=O(Tp)$; all $n$ input bits, including leading zeroes,
4504	are retained before the final group is padded.

4779	The carries satisfy $0\le k_j\le q(Q_0-1)<Q_0^2$.  If this holds at
4780	$j$, then
4781	\[
4782	 c_j+k_j\le q(Q_0-1)^2+q(Q_0-1)=qQ_0(Q_0-1),
4783	\]
4784	which proves the next carry bound.  The defining relation
4785	$c_j+k_j=d_j+Q_0k_{j+1}$ also gives the exact invariant
4786	\[
4787	 \sum_{h<j}c_hQ_0^h
4788	   =\sum_{h<j}d_hQ_0^h+k_jQ_0^j.
4789	\]
4790	It holds for $j=0$, and the defining relation proves its next instance.
4791	The unprocessed terms are multiples of $Q_0^j$, so the identity fixes
4792	the first $j$ radix digits of the full product.  The value $k_j$ is
4793	the carry from the processed coefficients into the remaining positions.
4794	
4795	After $\Phi^{-1}$ the coefficients occur in increasing ordinary index,
4796	so this carry scan proceeds from least to most significant.  Carry
4797	storage and work per coefficient are $O(b)$ bits and steps.  Write
4798	each digit's bits from low to high on a work tape, and drain the final
4799	$O(b)$-bit carry in the same order.  Copy the completed stream backward
4800	once to obtain most-significant-first order.  The stream has length
4801	$O(Sb)=O(Tp)$, including chunk padding and the final carry, so this
4802	reversal is a charged linear tape pass.  The exact product is less
4803	than $2^{2n}$; all bits above position $2n-1$ are therefore zero.
4804	Remove only those zero padding bits and retain leading zeros as needed
4805	to produce exactly $2n$ bits.  Zero inputs obey the same invariant and
4806	output rule.

4997	\label{sec:exact-arithmetic-proof}
4998	
4999	Let $n$ be the supplied input width, let $a$ be the nonnegative dividend
5000	or radicand, and let $b>0$ be the divisor for the division task, with
5001	the values and output conventions of Corollary~\ref{cor:exact-arithmetic}.
5002	Here $p\ge1$ denotes an integer target precision for a Newton routine.
5003	
5004	\begin{proof}[Proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:exact-arithmetic}]
5005	We use the classical Newton reductions as presented by
5006	Brent~\cite[Lemmas 2.1--2.4]{Brent1976}, with their tape costs made
5007	explicit. Set $B(p)=p(\lg p)^{1-\kappa}$. A linear scan handles a zero
5008	dividend or radicand and finds the significant bits of a positive input.
5009	For division write $b=2^h c$, where $0\le h<n$ and $1\le c<2$.
5010	For square root write $a=2^{2e}c$, where $0\le e<n/2$ and $1\le c<4$.
5011	Copy the normalized digits most significant first to a tape with a marked
5012	beginning. This initial scan also records the relevant exponent.
5013	
5014	For an integer $t\ge1$, let
5015	$R_t(z)=2^{-t}\lfloor 2^t z\rfloor$ and put $\delta=2^{-t}$.
5016	The prefix $c_t=R_t(c)$ has $0\le c-c_t<\delta$.
5017	Each product below is computed exactly on integer significands and
5018	then rounded by the indicated $R_t$; additions and shifts are exact
5019	until a stated rounding. When precision increases, the stored dyadic
5020	iterate is extended by zero fractional bits.
5021	
5022	For the reciprocal iteration $x\leftarrow x(2-cx)$, compute
5023	\[
5024	 u=R_t(c_t x),\qquad x^+=R_t\bigl(x(2-u)\bigr).
5025	\]
5026	Put $\varepsilon=1-cx$. If $|\varepsilon|\le1/2$, then
5027	$0<x\le3/2$. Writing $\eta_1=u-c_t x$ and
5028	$\eta_2=x^+-x(2-u)$ gives $|\eta_i|<\delta$ and
5029	\[
5030	 1-cx^+
5031	 =\varepsilon^2-c(c-c_t)x^2+cx\eta_1-c\eta_2.
5032	\]
5033	Since $cx^2=(1-\varepsilon)^2/c\le9/4$, $cx\le3/2$, and $c<2$,
5034	\[
5035	 |1-cx^+|
5036	 \le\varepsilon^2+\frac{23}{4}\delta
5037	 <\varepsilon^2+6\delta.                                  \tag{*}
5038	\]
5039	The fixed seed $x=5/8$ has $|\varepsilon|\le3/8$ throughout
5040	$1\le c<2$. One step with $t=6$ therefore gives residual less than
5041	$9/64+6/64=15/64<1/4$.
5042	
5043	For a requested target $p\ge1$, begin with $m=1$ after this warm-up.
5044	While $m<p$, set $m'=\min\{2m,p\}$ and work at $t=m'+5$ fractional
5045	bits. If the residual is at most $2^{-m-1}$, then $(*)$ gives
5046	\[
5047	 |1-cx^+|
5048	 \le2^{-2m-2}+6\,2^{-m'-5}
5049	 \le\frac7{16}\,2^{-m'}<2^{-m'-1}.
5050	\]
5051	Set $m=m'$ and continue. The reciprocal routine at target $p$ thus
5052	returns a dyadic $x$ satisfying
5053	$|1-cx|\le2^{-p-1}$ and $|x-1/c|\le2^{-p-1}$.
5054	These errors are measured against the true $c$ at every stage, although
5055	the prefix $c_t$ changes.
5056	
5057	For the root iteration $x\leftarrow(x+c/x)/2$, first suppose
5058	$1/2\le x\le5/2$. Normalize this stored dyadic exactly as $x=2^j d$,
5059	where $1\le d<2$ and $j\in\{-1,0,1\}$. The reciprocal routine at
5060	target $t$ returns $z$ with $|1-dz|\le2^{-t-1}$. Put $v=2^{-j}z$.
5061	Because $d\ge1$ and $2^{-j}\le2$, we have
5062	$|v-1/x|\le2^{-t}=\delta$. Compute the quotient and root update by
5063	\[
5064	 q_t=R_t(c_t v),\qquad x^+=R_t\bigl((x+q_t)/2\bigr).
5065	\]
5066	Here $c_t<4$ and $1/x\le2$, so the quotient has the uniform error
5067	\[
5068	 |q_t-c/x|
5069	 \le\delta+c_t|v-1/x|+\frac{|c_t-c|}{x}
5070	 \le7\delta.
5071	\]
5072	The exact Newton identity gives
5073	\[
5074	 |x^+-\sqrt c|
5075	 \le\frac{(x-\sqrt c)^2}{2x}+\delta+\frac12|q_t-c/x|
5076	 \le\frac{(x-\sqrt c)^2}{2x}+\frac92\delta.
5077	\]
5078	The fixed seed $x=3/2$ has $|x-\sqrt c|\le1/2$. At this seed the
5079	first term is at most $1/12$, so one step with $t=6$ has error less
5080	than $1/12+5/64<1/4$. Thereafter the invariant
5081	$|x-\sqrt c|\le2^{-m-1}$, with $m\ge1$, gives
5082	$3/4\le x\le9/4$ and hence supplies the denominator bound for the
5083	next step. Since $1/(2x)\le1$ and $9/2<6$, the same capped doubling
5084	schedule with five guard bits gives $|x-\sqrt c|\le2^{-p-1}$ at
5085	target $p$.

5088	step, $x\le3/2$ and $u\le c_t x\le3/2$ whenever $(*)$ is used. In a
5089	root step, $x\le5/2$, $v\le2+\delta<3$, and $q_t<12$. A fixed number
5090	of integer guard bits therefore suffices. At working precision $t$,
5091	each retained significand has $t+O(1)$ bits, including the fixed
5092	additional precision of the inner reciprocal, and each exact product
5093	has $2t+O(1)$ bits. Theorem~\ref{thm:main} applies to the padded
5094	significands. The streaming conventions give $O(t)$ cost for additions,
5095	shifts, copying, truncation and head returns.

5098	only the required prefix, and returns over that prefix. If the finite
5099	input ends first, the remaining fractional bits are zero. A root stage
5100	forms $d$ once in $O(t)$ time; each stage of its inner reciprocal routine

5102	rescans an entire longer input.

5105	$\sum_j(m_j+5)=O(p)$, and monotonicity of $\lg$ gives

5112	products, so the complete reciprocal routine at target $p$ costs
5113	$O(B(p))$. A root stage of working precision $t$ uses a reciprocal
5114	at target $t$ and one further product, and hence costs $O(B(t))$.

5116	sum to $O(p)$ at both levels.
5117	
5118	The outer registers and the reused reciprocal and multiplier tapes form
5119	one fixed finite tape set with fixed subroutine depth. Marking the ends
5120	of each call's visited intervals on fixed tracks permits those intervals
5121	to be cleared and their heads returned in a constant multiple of the
5122	call's running time. No random-access simulation is used.
5123

5127	the initial normalization scan, this accounts for the fixed-tape
5128	implementation. For division, the reciprocal routine gives

5132	\[

5150	 \section{A consequence for matrix transposition}
5151	\label{sec:transposition}
5152	
5153	For positive integers $n_1,n_2,b$, a row-major $n_1\times n_2$ array
5154	of $b$-bit strings stores
5155	entry $(i,j)$, where $0\le i<n_1$ and $0\le j<n_2$, at position
5156	$n_2i+j$; transposition places this string at position $n_1j+i$.
5157	Harvey and van der Hoeven prove that any multiplication machine with
5158	worst-case cost $M(m)$ yields a fixed multitape transposition machine with
5159	cost~\cite[Corollary~6.2]{HarveyHoeven2025}
5160	\[
5161	O\!\left(M(m)+m\lg\lg\max(n_1,n_2)\right),
5162	 \qquad n_1n_2b\le m.
5163	\]
5164	The cited transposition interface receives $m$ as well as $n_1,n_2,b$
5165	and the matrix stream~\cite[Section~1.1]{HarveyHoeven2025}. For the
5166	matrix problem defined here, compute $m=n_1n_2b$ from the three binary
5167	descriptors and supply all four parameters. The four descriptors have total length
5168	$O(\log(2m))$, and the two schoolbook products that compute $m$ cost
5169	$O(\log^2(2m))=O(m)$ steps.
5170	
5171	The cited multiplication interface likewise receives $m$ explicitly
5172	and two nonnegative operands smaller than $2^m$; it uses standard binary
5173	representations of the operands and product. On each such call, read the
5174	supplied $m$ and form two words
5175	of exactly $m$ bits, most significant bit first, by adding leading zeroes.
5176	Feed their $x\#y$ concatenation to Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Its final
5177	output pass writes the $2m$-bit product consecutively. Scan this block
5178	to remove leading zeroes, emitting one $0$ bit if every bit is zero.
5179	This fixes a canonical binary representation of the product.
5180	If a tape orientation requires reversal, read the stored word backward
5181	while writing it forward on a spare tape. Padding, normalization, and
5182	copying therefore cost $O(m)$ steps on a fixed number of tapes.
5183	
5184	Suppose the multiplication bound is $O(m(\lg m)^{1-\kappa})$ for a
5185	fixed $0<\kappa<1$.  Positivity of the dimensions and entry width gives
5186	$\max(n_1,n_2)\le n_1n_2b\le m$.  Hence
5187	\[
5188	 \lg\lg\max(n_1,n_2)\le\lg\lg m
5189	   =o((\lg m)^{1-\kappa}).
5190	\]
5191	The final relation uses $1-\kappa>0$; the bounded cases are absorbed
5192	using the stated convention for $\lg$.  Thus the cited transposition
5193	cost is $O(m(\lg m)^{1-\kappa})$.  Taking $m=n_1n_2b$ expresses this
5194	bound in matrix bits. In particular, an
5195	$n\times n$ binary matrix can be transposed in
5196	$O(n^2(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ time. Dimensions equal to one cause no
5197	exception, since our convention gives $\lg1=1$.

5205	spectator lengths. Each group is a complete rectangle, so the full
5206	rectangular algorithm, including its deterministic repair, can be applied
5207	to one group at a time. The only additional work is reading the group
5208	descriptors and passing consecutive groups through the same local tapes.
5209	
5210	\begin{definition}[Grouped packed stream]
5211	\label{def:grouped-packed-stream}
5212	Let $M,R\ge1$, $K\ge6$, $f\ge1$, $L=fK$, and $0\le\rho<K$.
5213	Fix an ordered template of $t\ge3$ two-bit tags: $\mathtt{00}$ denotes
5214	a spectator field, and $\mathtt{01},\mathtt{10},\mathtt{11}$ denote
5215	$x,y,z$, respectively. Each chunk tag occurs exactly once. The template
5216	is common to all $J\ge1$ groups of this input, but its length may vary
5217	between inputs. Group $\nu$ has a positive row count $n_\nu$ and a
5218	positive length $a_{\nu,h}$ at each spectator tag $h$; at a chunk tag
5219	put $a_{\nu,h}=2^L$. Define
5220	\[
5221	 Q_\nu=\prod_{h=1}^t a_{\nu,h},\qquad
5222	 M_\nu=n_\nu Q_\nu,\qquad
5223	 C_\nu=\sum_{\mu<\nu}M_\mu,\qquad V_\nu=M_\nu R,
5224	\]
5225	and require $M=\sum_{\nu=1}^J M_\nu$.
5226	
5227	The stream consists of $M$ records of $R$ bits. In group order, their
5228	addresses form the consecutive lexicographic rectangles
5229	\[
5230	 [n_\nu]\times\prod_{h=1}^t[a_{\nu,h}].
5231	\]
5232	The first coordinate is a row ordinal. Every row contains the full
5233	Cartesian suffix displayed above: no suffix length depends on a
5234	coordinate within that row. The suffix lengths may differ between
5235	groups. Every finite sequence of per-row spectator length vectors in
5236	the fixed template is representable, using groups of count one when
5237	necessary.
5238	
5239	Use the integer code $\Gamma$ from \eqref{eq:integer-descriptor-code}.
5240	The supplied descriptor
5241	is exactly
5242	\[
5243	\begin{split}
5244	 \mathcal D={}&
5245	 \Gamma(M)\Gamma(R)\Gamma(K)\Gamma(f)\Gamma(\rho+1)\Gamma(t)\,
5246	 T_1\cdots T_t\,\Gamma(J)\\
5247	 &{}\cdot\prod_{\nu=1}^{J}
5248	 \left(\Gamma(n_\nu)
5249	       \prod_{h:T_h=\mathtt{00}}\Gamma(a_{\nu,h})\right),
5250	\end{split}
5251	\]
5252	where $T_h$ is the tag at position $h$, and juxtaposition and products
5253	mean bitstring concatenation in increasing index order. The header,
5254	tag count, and group count delimit the entire list. A grouped packed
5255	stream is valid when this descriptor and its accompanying records have
5256	exactly the parameters, shapes, and orders just specified.
5257	\end{definition}
5258	
5259	\begin{lemma}[Packed selected-bit addition for grouped rectangles]
5260	\label{lem:packed-selected-bit-addition}
5261	Let a valid grouped packed stream of
5262	Definition~\ref{def:grouped-packed-stream} be supplied, and let $A\ge2$
5263	bound the actual total bit length of its descriptor $\mathcal D$,
5264	including the header and the entry for $R$. At the positions
5265	$j_i=\rho+iK$, numbered from the least significant bit, one fixed
5266	multitape procedure performs
5267	\[
5268	 y_{j_i}\longleftarrow y_{j_i}\mathbin\oplus x_{j_i}
5269	 \quad(0\le i<f)
5270	\]
5271	in every group. It fixes the group, row ordinal, spectator coordinates,
5272	all other chunk bits, and every record payload; in particular, the chunk
5273	$z$ is restored.
5274	For $V=MR$, its time is
5275	\begin{equation}
5276	\label{eq:packed-selected-time}
5277	 O\!\left(V(L^\tau+1)+MA^3+
5278	       M\min\{1,80(f-1)2^{-K}\}\,A(R+A)\right).
5279	\end{equation}
5280	When $A=O(p)$, $R$ exceeds every fixed polynomial in $p$,
5281	$f\le d\le p$, and $K/\log p\to\infty$, this is
5282	$O(V(L^\tau+1))$, uniformly over the group counts, shapes, and payloads
5283	whose supplied descriptors satisfy that bound.
5284	\end{lemma}
5285	
5286	\begin{proof}
5287	Write $s=t-3$ for the number of spectator tags. Each group explicitly
5288	stores $s+1$ positive integer codes, so $J(s+1)\le A$ and
5289	$Jt=J(s+3)\le3A$. Also $J\le M$, because every group is nonempty.
5290	The header includes $\Gamma(M)$ and $\Gamma(R)$, so
5291	$\log_2 M+\log_2 R=O(A)$. Every field length, partial suffix product,
5292	row count and group record count is at most $M$. These integers, as well
5293	as $V_\nu=M_\nu R$, therefore have $O(A)$ bits. In particular,
5294	\[
5295	 A_\nu:=\lceil\log_2(2V_\nu)\rceil=O(A)
5296	\]
5297	with a constant independent of the number and shapes of the groups.
5298	
5299	Parse the descriptor in forward group order, keeping the common template
5300	on a separate tape and saving the current group's length vector locally.
5301	Collapse the row ordinal and the spectator fields before the first chunk
5302	into one prefix field. Collapse each spectator interval between the chunks
5303	and after the last chunk in the same way; an empty interval has length
5304	one. The resulting four positive lengths $N_0,N_1,N_2,N_3$, together
5305	with the current order of the names $x,y,z$, give exactly the rectangle
5306	in Lemma~\ref{lem:packed-selected-bit-rectangle}, with $M_\nu$ records
5307	and volume $V_\nu$. Fixing a collapsed coordinate fixes every one of its
5308	mixed-radix factors. Hence the rectangular algorithm preserves the row
5309	ordinal and all original spectator coordinates, as the grouped claim
5310	requires.
5311	
5312	For each group, reading the template and length vector, forming the four
5313	products, and writing the local descriptor with its fixed number of
5314	entries take $O(A^3)$ time:
5315	there are $O(A)$ field visits and schoolbook operations, each on
5316	$O(A)$-bit integers. The descriptor supplied to the rectangular routine
5317	contains only its four collapsed lengths and $R,K,f,\rho$, in canonical
5318	binary, with the finite permutation of the three chunk names. The
5319	routine does not receive or rescan the outer group table.
5320	
5321	Use separate outer input and output tapes with forward cursors. Copy the
5322	$V_\nu$ bits of group $\nu$ into a local area, apply the complete
5323	rectangular algorithm there, append its output to the outer output tape,
5324	and clear the visited local area. Keep the outer cursors at their group
5325	boundaries during the local call. Reuse the same local and primitive work
5326	tapes for every group. The copy, append, positioning and cleanup cost
5327	$O(V_\nu)$; one final outer rewind costs $O(V)$. The inner routine
5328	restores its local work tapes as part of its stated bound. Thus the tape
5329	count is fixed, and no local call scans an earlier or later group.
5330	
5331	Put $\delta_{\rm bad}=\min\{1,80(f-1)2^{-K}\}$. Within group $\nu$,
5332	Lemma~\ref{lem:packed-selected-bit-rectangle} performs all the required
5333	XORs, restores $z$ for every initial value, and preserves each payload.
5334	Its exceptional records are extracted, sorted and reinserted entirely
5335	within that group. Their destination ranks therefore require only the
5336	local $A_\nu$-bit address bound; no ordering across groups is needed.
5337	The local time is
5338	\[
5339	 O\!\left(V_\nu(L^\tau+1)+M_\nu A_\nu^3+
5340	       \delta_{\rm bad}M_\nu A_\nu(R+A_\nu)\right).
5341	\]
5342	Summing these bounds and the descriptor work, using
5343	$\sum_\nu M_\nu=M$, $\sum_\nu V_\nu=V$, $A_\nu=O(A)$ and $J\le M$,
5344	gives
5345	\[
5346	 O\!\left(V(L^\tau+1)+MA^3+
5347	       \delta_{\rm bad}MA(R+A)\right),
5348	\]
5349	which is \eqref{eq:packed-selected-time}. This sum includes the whole
5350	record payload on every local exceptional-sort pass. The rectangular
5351	lemma also covers $f=1$, when its rotations and repair are empty.
5352	
5353	After division by $V=MR$, the two additional terms are bounded by
5354	$A^3/R$ and $80(f-1)2^{-K}A(1+A/R)$. Under the displayed family bounds,
5355	the first tends to zero, and the second is
5356	$O(p^2 2^{-K}(1+A/R))=o(1)$. These bounds depend on the supplied groups
5357	only through $M,R,A$, proving the asserted uniformity.
5358	\end{proof}
5359	 \bibliographystyle{plain}
5360	\bibliography{references}
5361	\end{document}

Turn source documents into a wiki of linked explanatory pages for a stated reader.

exegenius makes no model calls. It hands out tasks (`next`) for an agent such as Claude Code to do, and checks and applies the answers (`submit`).

Usage: exegenius [OPTIONS] [COMMAND]

Commands:
  init        Create exegenius.toml and sources/ if missing, and (re)write the Claude Code skill
  next        Print the current batch of tasks, or build the docs when nothing is left
  submit      Check and apply the answer to a task
  read        Open a wiki page for a pending simulated-reader task
  search      Search the wiki for a pending simulated-reader task
  background  Give the background task again, with a correction of what it said the reader knows (only right after `next` shows the background)
  status      Show progress
  plan        Print the pages needed to reach the target, in reading order
  build       Write docs/ and zensical.toml from the pages written so far
  help        Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -C, --dir <DIR>
          Project directory, containing exegenius.toml
          
          [default: .]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version
